Chapter 6 
INTEGRITY, VIGILANCE, TRANSPARENCY AND SERVICE 
MATTERS 
 
A. Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) 
6.0 The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is the premier investigating agency of the 
country entrusted with investigating cases of corruption, major economic offences, banking 
and financial frauds, and other serious conventional crimes. The Bureau also undertakes 
investigation of certain specialized and sensitive matters, including terrorist offences and 
cases of national importance. Cases are referred to the CBI by the Central Government, with 
the concurrence of the concerned State Governments where required, as well as by the 
Hon’ble High Courts and the Hon’ble Supreme Court. 
Human Resource Management 
6.1 The Committee notes that against a sanctioned strength of 7,300 posts, the in-position 
strength of CBI is 6,212, leaving a shortfall of 1,088 posts (14.90%). The rank-wise details of 
sanctioned strength, in-position strength and vacancies are placed at Annexure–I. While the 
Committee appreciates that the vacancy position has reduced from 20.57% in 2024 to 14.90% 
in 2025 and is projected to decline further, the Committee believes that a vacancy level of 
nearly fifteen per cent in a premier investigative agency remains a matter of serious concern.  
6.2 As per the information provided by the Department, the major reasons for vacancies 
are: 
i. CBI is not receiving sufficient & suitable nominations of officers from State Police 
which has traditionally been a major source of induction, particularly in the rank of 
Inspector & SPs; 
ii. Some candidates recommended by UPSC and SSC against the direct recruitment 
quota do not ultimately join the organization because of that there always remain 
some vacancies under Direct Recruitment Quota; 
iii. Delay in sending the relevant documents by lending departments after identifying the 
personnel by CBI for deputation; 
iv. Non identifying suitable / skilled personnel by the lending departments which results 
in non-selection of the personnel for induction even after scrutiny; 
v. There are vacancies in promotion quota because of non-availability of eligible 
officers. 

 
66 
6.3 The Committee notes that one of the major reasons for vacancies under the 
Direct Recruitment quota is that certain candidates recommended by UPSC and SSC 
do not ultimately join the organisation, resulting in persistent shortfalls. The Committee 
is of the view that such avoidable vacancies should not be allowed to spill over and affect 
operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a system of 
maintaining a reserve panel/waitlist, in consultation with the recruiting agencies, may 
be institutionalised so that vacancies arising due to this phenomenon can be filled in a 
time-bound manner without initiating a fresh recruitment cycle. 
6.4 The Committee further notes that as informed by the Department, there are 77 
vacancies out of 500 posts in the Sub-Inspector grade as on 31.12.2025. A high attrition rate 
has also been indicated in this cadre. Considering that Sub-Inspector is the feeder grade for 
supervisory positions and forms the backbone of investigation work, the Committee views 
this as a matter of serious concern. While the Committee acknowledges the earlier reforms in 
Recruitment Rules and introduction of the Limited Departmental Competitive Examination 
(LDCE) to improve career progression, it notes that some structural challenges in cadre 
management continue to persist. 
6.5 The Committee recommends that a detailed root cause analysis be undertaken to 
examine the reasons for attrition in the SI cadre, including issues relating to workload, 
career progression, working conditions, transfers, training, and inter-organisational 
mobility. Based on such analysis, appropriate corrective measures may be introduced to 
enhance retention and morale. 
6.6 The Committee emphasizes that sustained and coordinated efforts are necessary to 
reduce vacancies to minimal levels so that the operational efficiency, investigative capacity 
and institutional credibility of the CBI are not compromised. 
 
Centralized Case Management System (CCMS) 
6.7 The Committee is pleased to note that the CCMS has been made functional within the 
Bureau and contains details of all cases being handled by the CBI. Additionally, certain non-
sensitive information such as searches, arrests, filing of charge-sheets and convictions is 
being periodically placed in the public domain through the CBI website. The Committee also 
appreciates that in compliance with the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, 
FIRs are being uploaded on the CBI website and FIRs involving searches are uploaded after 
their completion, in order to maintain confidentiality. 

 
67 
6.8 However, the Committee observes that the core issue underlying its earlier 
recommendations made in the 122nd, 126th and 145th Reports, such as, structured and 
systematic public disclosure of consolidated case statistics and publication of the CBI’s 
Annual Report in the public domain, remains unaddressed. While selective updates are 
posted on the website, these do not substitute for comprehensive, periodic statistical 
disclosures that would enable meaningful public understanding of pendency, disposal 
rates, conviction rates and category-wise case status. 
6.9 In a bid to strengthen institutional accountability, the Committee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the CBI should place its Annual Report in the public 
domain with appropriate safeguards for classified or sensitive information; and develop 
a comprehensive framework for periodic publication of consolidated and non-sensitive 
case statistics, including data on registration, pendency, disposal and conviction rates. 
Moreover, a clear timeline be indicated for the public interface of the Centralized Case 
Management System. 
CBI Courts 
6.10 During the deliberations, the Committee was apprised of the current practice about the 
posting of senior-level judges in CBI-designated Courts,which results in limited tenures due 
to their superannuation. Such short tenures, particularly at the senior level, may result in 
disruption of judicial continuity, loss of familiarity with voluminous records and technical 
evidence, and consequent delays in trial proceedings, particularly in complex corruption and 
economic offence matters. 
6.11 The Committee is of the view that specialized courts dealing with CBI cases 
require stability and judicial continuity to ensure timely adjudication and effective 
prosecution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department, in 
consultation with the concerned High Courts, explore the feasibility of ensuring a 
reasonable and fixed tenure for judicial officers posted to CBI-designated Courts. The 
Committee further recommends that junior and mid-level judges may be posted to such 
Courts for an adequate duration so as to ensure continuity and development of domain 
expertise. 
Cybercrime 
6.12 The Committee notes with serious concern the growing menace of cybercrime, 
particularly cases where fraudsters impersonate officers of premier investigative agencies, 

 
68 
including the CBI and intimidate victims through threats of legal action, arrest or financial 
penalties, thereby coercing them to transfer money. The Committee observes that senior 
citizens are especially vulnerable to such tactics due to limited digital literacy, lack of 
familiarity with cyber fraud methods and heightened susceptibility to fear-based 
manipulation. Such impersonation not only causes financial and emotional distress to victims 
but also risks undermining public trust in investigative institutions. 
6.13 The Committee recommends that the CBI, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and State Governments, undertake targeted public awareness campaigns, 
particularly in regional languages and through platforms accessible to senior citizens, 
clarifying that the Bureau does not demand money or conduct investigations through 
unofficial digital channels. The Committee further recommends strengthening rapid-
response mechanisms in coordination with banks and digital payment platforms to 
enable immediate freezing of suspected fraudulent transactions. Moreover, the 
Committee underscores the need for enhancing inter-agency coordination to dismantle 
organized cyber fraud networks impersonating public officials, and continuously 
upgrading the capacity of investigating officers in emerging cybercrime domains, 
including digital forensics and crypto currency-related offences. 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
6.14 The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) is the apex integrity institution responsible 
for tendering advice on vigilance matters relating to the Central Government and its 
organisations. It exercises jurisdiction over all matters to which the executive power of the 
Union extends. The Commission functions as an independent statutory body. 
Granting Prosecution Sanctions under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 
6.15 The Committee notes that delays continue to be observed in the grant of prosecution 
sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. As informed by the Commission, 
such delays are often attributed to requests for clarifications from investigating agencies or 
administrative authorities before a decision is taken on sanction proposals. While the 
Committee appreciates that periodic review meetings are held by CVC with the CBI and 
guidelines have been issued by DoPT to minimize delays, the issue of timely and accountable 
decision-making in prosecution sanctions remains a matter of concern. 
6.16 The Committee further recalls that in its 145th Report (Para 6.15), it had 
recommended the establishment of a Centralized Digital Case Repository (CDCR) for secure 

 
69 
storage and instant retrieval of case records, along with mandatory timelines and 
accountability mechanisms for administrative authorities. In response, CVC had stated that 
MeitY’s DigiLocker platform may serve as a repository framework and that the 
recommendation would be taken up with MeitY.  
6.17  The Committee notes that there are delays in prosecution sanction and 
recommends that the Commission, in coordination with DoPT and MeitY, provide an 
updated status on the proposed Centralized Digital Case Repository. The Committee 
may be apprised of the present status of consultations with MeitY regarding integration 
with DigiLocker or any alternative digital repository system. Further, the Committee 
desires that a clear timeline be indicated for full operationalization of a digital tracking 
and repository mechanism to ensure expeditious and transparent disposal of 
prosecution sanction cases.

6.20 Moreover, the Vigilance Manual prescribes specific timelines, including three months

data has been furnished to indicate adherence to these timelines or to identify the stage at 
which maximum delay occurs. In the absence of investigation-stage pendency data, the 

 
70 
Committee is unable to ascertain whether advisory-stage pendency is a downstream effect of 
delayed investigations and protracted departmental inquiries. 
6.21 The Committee recommends that the Commission, in exercise of its supervisory 
and review functions, furnish consolidated stage-wise data for the last three years 
indicating the average time taken at key stages of vigilance processing, including 
investigation, reference to the Commission, consideration of advice, and issuance of 
final orders, based on information available with it or received from 
Ministries/Departments. The Commission may also indicate the number of cases 
pending beyond the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual at stages that require 
its review or advisory intervention. Such data would enable a clearer understanding of 
systemic delays and trends in vigilance administration. 
6.22 The Committee is pleased to note that the Commission has developed the 
Vigilance Case Management System (VCMS) to monitor receipt, disposal and 
implementation of its advice. The Committee recommends the VCMS may be further 
leveraged to incorporate comprehensive stage-wise tracking of cases from the stage of 
complaint and investigation at the departmental level through inquiry, Commission 
advice and final disposal, with automated flagging of cases pending beyond the timelines 
prescribed in the Vigilance Manual. Periodic analytical reports may be generated from 
the system to identify recurring bottlenecks across Ministries and organizations. Such 
enhanced monitoring would help detect systemic delays early and promote compliance 
with the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual. 
Uniformity in Vigilance Frameworks across Public Sector Entities 
6.23 The Committee takes note of certain challenges faced by the Commission in ensuring 
uniform implementation of vigilance instructions across CPSEs, Public Sector Banks, Public 
Sector Insurance Companies and other autonomous bodies. These include the lack of an 
effective and structured vigilance set-up and non-appointment of Chief Vigilance Officers in 
Joint Ventures, Special Purpose Vehicles and subsidiaries; uneven or absent provisions in 
certain CPSEs for initiating or continuing disciplinary proceedings against retired employees; 
and lack of uniformity in service regulations of PSBs and PSICs, particularly in dealing with 
composite cases. 
6.24 The Committee recommends that the Commission, in consultation with the 
concerned Ministries and regulatory authorities, undertake a structured review of these 
gaps and issue appropriate advisories to promote greater uniformity in vigilance 

 
71 
frameworks across CPSEs, banks, insurance companies and their subsidiaries. 
Particular attention may be given to ensuring structured vigilance set-ups in JVs/SPVs 
and subsidiaries, harmonisation of provisions relating to action against retired 
employees, and standardisation of service regulations dealing with composite cases, so 
as to strengthen consistency and effectiveness in vigilance administration. 
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
6.25 The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established in 1985 to provide 
speedy and cost-effective redressal to government employees aggrieved by decisions relating 
to service matters. The Tribunal adjudicates service-related disputes that were earlier dealt 
with by courts up to and including the High Courts. At present, CAT functions through 19 
regular Benches across the country, including its Principal Bench at Delhi. 
Pendency of Cases Pending for More than Ten Years 
6.26 The Committee acknowledges that the number of cases pending for more than ten 
years has shown a gradual decline, decreasing from 1,394 cases as on 31.12.2023 to 1,321 
cases as on 31.12.2024 and further to 1,238 cases as on 31.12.2025. However, the number of 
such cases remains significant. The Tribunal has informed that the key constraints in disposal 
of such long-pending matters include the following: 
cases adjourned sine-die due to related matters being sub-judice before the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court or High Courts; cases restored or remanded after long intervals while 
retaining their original institution dates; matters initially dismissed in default and 
subsequently restored; and repeated adjournments sought by counsel for filing replies or 
rejoinders. 
6.27 The Committee further notes that while special drives are conducted from time to 
time based on pendency assessment, there is no proposal to institutionalize such drives as a 
regular mechanism. Given the age of these cases, their prolonged pendency undermines 
timely access to justice, particularly in service and pension-related matters. 
6.28 The Committee is conscious of the judicial and procedural constraints that may 
affect the disposal of certain long-pending cases. However, the continued pendency of 
cases for more than ten years remains a matter of serious concern and warrants priority 
attention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Tribunal adopt a structured 
and periodic review mechanism for such cases, with focused listing and appropriate 
time-bound disposal strategies, to the extent feasible within the existing legal 

 
72 
framework. While special drives may continue as required, the monitoring of cases 
pending for over ten years may be institutionalised through regular review at the level 
of the Chairman to ensure sustained reduction in pendency and to prevent 
accumulation of similarly aged cases in future. 
Status of operationalizing the Advance Case Information System (ACIS) in CAT 
6.29 The Committee notes with appreciation that the work of scanning and 
digitization of judicial records is being carried out in a phased manner across all 
Benches of CAT, and that implementation of the Document Management System (DMS) 
in the Principal Bench was tentatively targeted for July, 2025, with full roll-out across 
all Benches expected by December, 2025. The Committee commends the progress made 
towards operationalizing a paperless and digitally enabled judicial system. In this 
regard, the Committee may be apprised of the current status of completion of 
digitization across Benches, operationalization of DMS (including e-Court/Smart Court 
components), and whether the targeted timelines have been adhered to. The Committee 
would also like to know the impact, if any, of ACIS implementation on case 
management efficiency and disposal rates thus far. 
Central Information Commission 
6.30 The Central Information Commission (CIC) was constituted by the Central 
Government under Section 12 of the Right to Information Act, 2005. The Commission 
comprises one Chief Information Commissioner and ten Information Commissioners, and 
was formally established through a Gazette Notification dated 11 October 2005. The CIC 
exercises the powers and performs the functions assigned to it under the Act to ensure 
effective implementation of the right to information framework.

it had appreciated the efforts made by the Commission to fill vacancies in the ASO and SA 
grades through SSC, but had expressed concern regarding the delay in revival of 48 deemed

AppCoMS and Technological Upgradation 
6.35 The Committee is pleased to note that the Appeal and Complaint Monitoring System 
(AppCoMS) has contributed to improving efficiency in registration, hearing and disposal of 
cases by enabling real-time tracking and streamlined case management. However, certain 
limitations have been identified by CIC, including absence of secure user authentication and 
lack of dedicated modules for early hearing and time-barred cases. These gaps are proposed 
to be addressed through the upgraded AppCoMS 2.0. 
6.36 As a step to plug the existing gaps, the Committee recommends that AppCoMS 
2.0 be implemented in a time-bound manner, incorporating secure authentication

Lokpal 
6.37 The Lokpal is a statutory anti-corruption institution established under the Lokpal and 
Lokayuktas Act, 2013 to inquire into allegations of corruption against specified public 

 
74 
functionaries within its jurisdiction. In accordance with Section 3(2) of the Act, the Lokpal 
comprises a Chairperson and up to eight Members, including both judicial and non-judicial 
Members. 
Constitution of the Inquiry Wing, Prosecution Wing and a Special Court 
 
6.38 The Committee recalls its earlier recommendation in its 145th and 159th reports that 
the Inquiry Wing and Prosecution Wing of the Lokpal be fully constituted within six months 
to enable effective discharge of its statutory mandate.  
6.39 With regard to the Inquiry Wing, the Committee notes that under Sections 10 and 11

headed by a Director of Inquiry for conducting preliminary inquiries. The Committee further 
notes that the Inquiry Wing has been formally constituted pursuant to resolutions of the Full

case basis.

6.41 With regard to prosecution, the Committee notes that the Prosecution Wing of

prosecution mechanism. While taking note of the constitution of the Prosecution Wing, 
the Committee desires to be apprised of the present stage of operationalization of the 
Prosecution Wing and the proposed roadmap for making it fully functional in 
accordance with the statutory framework.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2026-27) OF THE

1. The Committee notes that during 2023-24 and 2024-25, Revised Estimates 
exceeded Budget Estimates by 13.0% and 10.6% respectively, yet actual 
expenditure fell short of the Revised Estimates by 5.43% and 2.59%. Further, in

projected outlays over the last five years. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive review of its budget 
formulation and expenditure management processes. The Committee is also of 
the view that greater realism in projections and improved execution discipline 
would enhance fiscal credibility and strengthen the Ministry’s case during pre-
budget consultations.                      (Para 2.9) 
2. The Committee notes that the performance of the three Departments of the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on the fiscal front needs 
to be improved. While DoPT has utilized only 75% of the funds allocated to it till

guidelines issued by the Ministry of Finance, expenditure in the last quarter of 
the financial year should ordinarily not exceed 33 per cent of the total Budget 
Estimates, and expenditure during the month of March should not exceed 15 per 
cent of the total Budget Estimates. In this context, the Committee emphasizes 
that the Department(s) must ensure that expenditure during the remaining 
months of the financial year is planned and paced in a manner consistent with 
these prescribed norms.                  (Para 2.15) 
3. The Committee notes that the average rate of expenditure across attached and 
subordinate offices stands at approximately 73.45 per cent as on 31 January 
2026. Considering that ten months of the financial year have elapsed, this reflects

considerable variation in utilisation levels across organisations. In particular, the 
Staff Selection Commission (50.45 per cent) and the Institute of Secretariat 

 
79 
Training and Management (56 per cent) have recorded utilisation levels 
significantly below the desirable benchmark, with substantial unspent balances 
remaining.                      (Para 2.18)

(from ₹515.15 crore (BE) to ₹548.50 crore (RE)), only 50.45 per cent of the funds 
have been utilized as on 31 January 2026, leaving an unspent balance of ₹271.79

5. The Committee believes that projections must be firmly aligned with the 
expenditure trends and the ability of the organization to utilize the funds within 
the financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should strengthen quarterly expenditure system monitoring and ensure strict 
adherence to the Ministry of Finance guidelines regarding even pacing of 
expenditure. As reflected in Table IX, the average utilization across 
organizations stands at 73.45 per cent as on 31 January 2026, with certain 
organizations such as the Staff Selection Commission (50.45 per cent) and the

stage for 2026-27, organizations such as Lokpal received only 20.24 per cent of 
their projected outlay, while ISTM and LBSNAA received 48.47 per cent and 
52.68 per cent respectively (Table X). The Committee is of the view that closer 
alignment between projections, Revised Estimates and actual utilization is 
essential. Upward revisions at the Revised Estimates stage without proportionate

  I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to 
submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred Sixty First Report           
on Demands for Grants 2026-27 pertaining to the Department of Administrative Reforms & 
Public Grievances and Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare  (Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances & Pensions). 
 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India projected under various 
Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year need to be voted by the Parliament. 
Subsequently, the Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred 
to concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close scrutiny 
thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Cou ncil of 
States. While making scrutiny of Demands for Grants, the Committee has made an appraisal 
of performance, programmes, schemes and policies of the D epartment of Administrative 
Reforms & Public Grievances and Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfar e vis-à-vis 
expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India. 
 
3. In the Report, scrutiny of Demand No. 74 pertaining to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances and Department of Pension & Pensioners' 
Welfare for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by the Committee.

CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENTS 
MINISTRY 
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the coordinating agency 
of the Central Government in personnel matters especially for issues concerning recruitment, 
training, career development, staff welfare as well as to the post retirement dispensation.  
1.1 The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT); 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG); and 
(iii) Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DoPPW). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1.2 The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Hon‘ble Prime Minister 
assisted by the Minister of State. The Department of Personnel and Training is functioning 
under the charge of an independent Secretary while the Department of Administrative 
Reforms & Public Grievances and the Department of Pension and Pensioners‘ Welfare are 
functioning under the charge of another Secretary. This report pertains to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances; and the Department of Pension and 
Pensioners‘ Welfare. 
 
 
 
 


 
2 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND  
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES (DARPG) 
 
Evolution of the Department 
1.3 In March, 1954, an Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was set up in Cabinet 
Secretariat as a follow up to one of the recommendations made by Paul H. Appleby. In 
March, 1964, a Department of Administrative Reforms was set up within the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was transferred to its charge 
from the Cabinet Secretariat. On 7th February, 1973, the work relating to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms was transferred to Department of Personnel created under Cabinet 
Secretariat on 1st August, 1970 and was re-designated as Department of Personnel and 
Administrative Reforms. In April, 1977, the Department of Personnel and Administrative 
Reforms was shifted from Cabinet Secretariat to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March 
1985, the Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms was elevated to a full fledged 
Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative Reforms, Public Grievances and 
Pensions. On 10th December, 1985 Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative 
Reforms, Public Grievances and Pensions was re-designated as the Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances and Pensions with three Departments namely, Department of Personnel 
and Training (DOPT), Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and 
Department of Pension and Pensioners Welfare. 
About the Department 
1.4 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal 
agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as for redressal of 
public grievances relating to the States in general and grievances pertaining to Central 
Government agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on important 
activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal 
through publications and documentation. The Department also undertakes activities in the 
field of international exchange and cooperation to promote public service reforms. There are 
8 Divisions in the Department namely Administrative Reforms, Organization & Methods, e-
Governance, Documentation & Dissemination, International Exchange & Cooperation, 
Administration & Coordination, Public Grievances and Administrative Reforms Commission 
(ARC)/e-Office. The Department comes under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances 
and Pensions and is headed by a Secretary. 
Functions of the Department 
1.5 As per the Government of India Allocation of Business Rules, the following subjects 
have been allocated to the Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances: 
(i) Administrative Reforms, including e-governance and dissemination of best 
  practices. 
(ii) Organization and Methods. 
(iii) Policy, coordination and monitoring of issues relating to: 
(a)  Redress of public grievances in general; and 
(b)  Grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies. 

 
3 
(c) Monitoring of implementation of e-Office in Central Ministries /   
  Departments. 
(iv) (a)  Research in public management; 
       (b)  Liaison with State Governments, professional institutions etc. in public 
   management matters. 
(v) Administration of Central Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure.  
 
1.6 Accordingly, the functions of the Department are as under:  
i. Matters relating to administrative reforms. 
ii. Organization of Civil Services Day and Prime Minister‘s Award for 
Excellence in Public Administration. 
iii. Capacity building, change management, and Government Process Re-
engineering to provide reform through e-governance. 
iv. e-Office Mission Mode Project under National e-Governance Plan (NeGP). 
v. Organization of National Conference on e-Governance and National awards 
on e-Governance. 
vi. Management of Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism. 
vii. Documentation and dissemination of Good Governance Practices-innovations, 
adaptation and replication.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR GOOD GOVERNANCE (NCGG) 
1.8 National Centre for Good Governance was established as an autonomous institute 
under the aegis of the Department of Personnel and Training by upgrading the erstwhile 
National Institution of Administrative Research, Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of 
Administration, Mussoorie. DARPG has been made the Administrative authority for NCGG 
since 08.11.2017. 
  
1.9 The Centre is envisaged to be the apex think-tank that would guide the Government 
and help in implementing good Governance reforms. It seeks to be a high-level institute for 
research and capacity building to deal with the entire gamut of governance issues from the 
National to State to the local level and in sectors across the Government. 
 
1.10 NCGG is governed by a Governing Body, under the Chairmanship of the Cabinet 
Secretary, GoI and a Management Committee with the Secretary of the Department as the 
Chairperson.  
Objectives of NCGG 
1.11 Following are the objectives of the NCGG:  
 To be a think tank for governance & policy reforms, cutting across 
administrative, social, economic and financial spheres. 
 To function as a national repository on information on best practices, initiatives 
and methodologies that promote Good Governance, E-Governance, innovation 
& change management within the government; 
 To initiate and participate in action research and capacity building on various 
aspects of regulatory and development administration, public policy, governance 
and public management at National/State & local levels; 
 To advise on key issues in governance and development synergy across various 
Ministries/ Departments of GoI, and State Governments; 
 To promote sharing and replication of innovative ideas and best practices in 
Governance.  
 To interact with national and international organizations, in and outside 
government, engaged in research and capacity building in the above spheres.  
 
Mandate of NCGG 
1.12 The mandate of the NCGG is to promote Good Governance by:  
 Carrying out Action Research/ Studies on issues relating to governance. 
 Capacity Building on Public Policy and Governance at both National and 
International level. 
 Organizing consultations, workshops, seminars/webinars & talks to promote 
improved governance. 
 Undertaking initiatives for citizen centric governance.

DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE 
(DPPW) 
About the Department 
1.13 The Department of Pension &  Pensioners' Welfare was set up in 1985 as part of the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions to formulate policy and coordination 
of matters relating to retirement benefits of Central Government employees. The Department 
started functioning  independently with effect from 01.04.2007. The sanction process and 
implementation of the pension policy is done by the respective Central Ministry/Department. 
This Department further, from time to time, simplifies the rules/guidelines and procedure to 
facilitate welfare of pensioners. All the Ministries/Departments falling under the jurisdiction 
of the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) are governed by the pension policy framed by 
this Department. However, Defence, Railways, Post and Telecom have their own processing 
and sanctioning mechanism for pension. The expenditure incurred on pension is directly dealt 
with by the Controller General of Accounts, M/o Finance for Central Government employees 
other than Defence, Railway, Post and Telecom. The Departme nt also receives a large 
number of references from Ministries/Departments and renders advice on interpretation of 
Pension Rules which govern Central Civil service.  
Functions of the Department 
1.14 The Allocation of Business Rules broadly allocates the followin g areas of work to the 
Department:- 
(i) Formulation of policy and co -ordination of matters relating to retirement benefits to 
Central Government employees. 
(ii) Administration of - 
 the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 2021; 
 the Central Civil Services (Implementation of National Pension System) 
Rules, 2021; 
 the Central Civil Services (Payment of Gratuity under National Pension 
System) Rules, 2021; 
 the Central Civil Services (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981; 
 the Central Civil Services (Extraordinary Pension) Rules, 1939; 
 any other scheme relating to Central Government pensioners, entrusted to the 
Department. 
(iii) Pension structure and relief to pensioners. 
(iv) New facilities of fringe benefits to the Central Government pensioners. 
(v) Matters relating to amendment to, or relaxation of, Pension rules or any other rule 
concerning retirement benefits. 
(vi) Policy and co-ordination relating to welfare of Central Government Pensioners. 
(vii) Matters with financial implication shall be subjec t to the concurrence of the Ministry 
of Finance. 
(viii) Action in respect of other matters involving recurring financial implications by way of 
relaxation or liberalization of any rule shall be subject, to guidelines, as agreed to 
between the Department of  Pension and Pensioners‘ Welfare and the Ministry of 
Finance, Department of Expenditure.

2.11 In order to improve budget utilisation and enhance the credibility of projections, 
the Committee recommends that the Department should undertake a rigorous internal 
review of its past three years’ schemes and activities, identifying specific heads and 
projects where slippages occurred and preparing realistic activity-wise timelines so that 
future BEs are based on clearly phased implementation plans rather than broad 
aggregate estimates. 
 
2.12 The Committee further recommends that the Department may strengthen its 
quarterly monitoring mechanism, with clearly defined physical and financial milestones 
and periodic mid-year reviews, so that emerging underspending is identified early and 
corrective measures such as re-appropriation within heads, timely re-allocation, or 
expediting pending approvals can be taken to minimise the gap between BE, RE and 
actual expenditure. 
 
2.13 The Committee also recommends that, while formulating projections for 
submission to the Ministry of Finance, the Department should base its proposals on 
demonstrable past utilisation, realistic assessment of implementation capacity and 
firmed-up project pipelines, so that the difference between projections and finally 
approved BEs, as well as subsequent revisions, is narrowed and the credibility of the 
Department’s budgetary demand gets enhanced.

Empowered Committee then makes its recommendations for the consideration of the Hon'ble

States/UTs to assess impact of various interventions made by the Central and State

proposed to be taken up during the next financial year 2025-26.

2.58 The DGGI represents next generation administrative reform in bench -marking 
governance at District level and is expected to provide guidance to the State as well as the 
District administration and other stakeholders in their eﬀorts to address existing gaps, plan to 
bridge these gaps and aid as decision making tool. The ranking brings healthy competition 
amongst districts in their quest to provide citizen centric administration and governance. The 
first ever District Good Governance Index (DGGI) for Jammu and  Kashmir encompassing 
10 Governance Sectors and 58 indicators was released on 22nd January, 2022.  
 
2.59 This was the first attempt of benchmarking Governance at Districts which  are the 
basic unit for administration and governance. Subsequently, more states have come forward 
to undertake DGGI in collaboration with DARPG. In furtherance of the achievement of 
releasing for Jammu & Kashmir, in 2023 -24 DARPG released DGGIs for the St ates of 
Gujarat on 21st May 2023; Arunachal Pradesh on 8th June 2023 and Maharashtra on 26th 
December 2024 in collaboration with the State Governments concerned. 
 
2.60 The Committee appreciates  the efforts of the Department in conceptualizing 
and implementing t he District Good Governance Index (DGGI)  as a progressive 
initiative towards benchmarking governance performance at the district level. The 
Committee notes that this innovative measure has introduced a spirit of healthy 
competition among districts and has provided a valuable framework for identifying 
gaps and promoting citizen -centric governance. The Committee , therefore,  
recommends that DGGI be expanded to more States, with particular attention to 
aspirational districts and those with high grievance loads, so that district -level 
competition and data-driven governance are strengthened where they are needed most.

PART-B: COMPREHENSIVE SYSTEM FOR REDRESSAL OF PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES  
 
1. Centralised Public Grievances Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) 
 
2.94 The Centralised Public Grievances Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) 
constitutes one of the most widely utilised Information Technology platforms in the country, 
providing direct access to citizens for approaching Government authorities. Citizens are 
enabled to file and track their grievances through CPGRAMS on a 24x7 basis. All Ministries 
and Departments of the Government of India, as well as State Governments, fo rm part of this 
comprehensive system. Public grievances serve as direct feedback from citizens regarding the 
performance of Government programmes, policies, and service delivery mechanisms. The 
Department has informed the Committee that effective utilisati on of this information can 
enhance accountability and efficiency in governance. 
 
2.95 The Department is currently engaged in comprehensive improvement of the Public 
Grievance redressal system, including a complete overhaul of its technology architecture 
through Next Generation technology solutions. The key activities encompass: developing a 
new technological solution for CPGRAMS; strengthening data analytics capability; capacity 
building of Grievance Redressal Officers; and creating awareness and enhancing outre ach of 
the public grievance platform. 
 
STRATEGIC BUILDING BLOCKS 
2.96 Advanced IT Infrastructure:  The Government has invested in next generation 
technology to enhance user experience in grievance registration, tracking, and monitoring. 
The new platform is being developed and operated by a System Integrator, M/s Accenture 
Solutions Pvt. Ltd., selected through a Request for Proposal (RFP) process, under the 
supervision of the National Informatics Centre (NIC). The Department is collaborating 
closely with all stakeholders including the Prime Minister's Office, Cabinet 
Secretariat/Directorate of Public Gri evances, Department of Posts, Pensions and Welfare, as 
well as all Central Ministries/Departments and State/Union Territory Governments for 
development of NextGen CPGRAMS. 
 
2.97 Data Analytics Capability: For data analytics, the Department has established a Data 
Strategy Unit in DARPG. Two dashboards, namely the Intelligent Grievance Monitoring 
System (IGMS) and Tree Dashboard, have been developed in collaboration with the Indian 
Institute of Technology, Kanpur, and the National Institute of Smart Governance (NI SG) 
respectively. The deliverables comprise Analytical Reports and Root Cause Analysis. 
 
OUTREACH AND AWARENESS:  
 
2.98 Creating awareness and publicity of the platform is critical to enhance its outreach. 
The Government is working with All India Radio, Doordarshan News, Common Service 
Centres, and Feedback Call Centres to expand the reach of CPGRAMS.  Capacity Building: 
Capacity Building of Grievance Redressal Officers is key to meaningful and quality redressal 
of grievances. The Government has collaborated with State Administrative Training Institutes 
(ATIs) under the SEVOTTAM Scheme of DARPG for capacity building of GROs in States. 

 
29 
2.99 The i-GOT Karmayogi platform and the Indian Society of Training and Management 
(ISTM) are also being leveraged for training and capacity building of GROs of Central 
Ministries. The Department has also initiated training of Grievance Redressal Officers of the 
Central Government in collaboration with the National Centre for Good Governance (NCGG) 
under the Sevottam Scheme. 
Compliance with Parliamentary Committee Recommendations 
2.100 The Parliamentary Standing Committee's 106th Report (Para 7.9) had recommended 
publicising the CPGRAMS portal through all possible means including the print and 
electronic media so that the benefits of the grievance redressal mechanism percolate down to 
those at the bottom of the pyramid.  In compliance with the aforesaid recommendation, 
DARPG made two short duration films in Hindi and English on CPGRAMS through the 
National Film Development Corporation (NFDC). 
 
2.101 The Committee appreciates  the efforts of the Department  for producing two 
short-duration films in Hindi and English on the CPGRAMS portal through the 
National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) to enhance public awareness about 
the grievance redr essal mechanism.  However, the Committee observes that there 
appears to be a lack of awareness among the masses regarding the availability and 
utility of these films. 
 
2.102 The Committee , therefore,  recommends that the Department undertake 
comprehensive advertising campaigns especially using digital media and social media to 
widely disseminate these films and ensure that the benefits of the CPGRAMS portal 
reach the common citizen, as the purpose of creating such films would otherwise remain 
largely unfulfilled. 
NEXTGEN CPGRAMS PROJECT

I. Digital Life Certificate (DLC) Campaign 4.0 
3.11. The DLC Campaign 4.0 was the largest ever campaign conducted for improving 
pensioners welfare in India from November 1 to 30, 2025 in 2000 cities/ towns across the 
Nation with 75000 camps and 1400 Nodal Officers, generated 1.78 crore Digital 
Life Certificates (DLCs). Over 1.07 Crore DLCs representing more than 60 percent were 
generated using face authentication technology, 2.5 times increase over the DLC 3.0 
Campaign. This proved particularly beneficial for elderly pensioners with faded fingerprints, 
differently abled individuals facing mobility challenges and pensioners liv ing in rural and 
remote areas. 13.05 lakh DLC‘s submitted by pensioners aged 80 and above, 24.87 lakh 
DLCs generated by State Bank of India, 3.52 lakh DLCs generated by IPPB and 3.38 lakh 
DLCs were generated by PNB.  
 
3.12. The Committee notes that submission of  Digital Life Certificate (DLC) through the 
Jeevan Pramaan Portal is mandatory for continuation and release of pension and financial 
assistance under various pension schemes, including schemes such as the Financial 
Assistance for Veteran Artists administer ed by the Ministry of Culture. The Committee 
observes that failure to submit DLC within the prescribed timeframe may result in stoppage 
or delay in release of pension or financial assistance to beneficiaries. 
 
3.13. The Committee notes that certain vulnerable and special categories of 
pensioners, including retired artisans, senior citizens, super senior citizens, pensioners 
residing in remote and far-flung areas, persons with limited access to digital technology, 
and those with low levels of digital literacy or general literacy, may not be fully aware of 
the requirement of submitting DLC or the procedure for doing so. The Committee is of 
the view that such pensioners may face hardship due to lack of awareness and 
technological barriers, r esulting in avoidable disruption in receipt of their rightful 
pension or financial assistance. 
 
3.14. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department undertake targeted 
and inclusive awareness campaigns specifically aimed at vulnerable and special 
categories of pensioners, including retired artisans, elderly pensioners, and pensioners 
residing in remote and rural areas. These awareness initiatives should focus on 
educating pensioners about the mandatory requirement of submitting Digital Life 
Certificates, the timelines involved, and the various available methods for submitting 
DLC, including face authentication, mobile-based submission, and assisted modes. 
 
3.15. The Committee further suggests  that such awareness campaigns be conducted 
through multiple outreach channels, including pensioner welfare associations, Common 
Service Centres (CSCs), banks, post offices, local administrative offices and field -level 
functionaries. Special assistance mechanisms may also be established to facilitate 
submission of DLC for pensioners with limited digital access or mobility constraints.

V. Pension Adalats 
 
3.21. Four Pension Adalats were organized on 13.02.2025,  4.06.2025, 10.09.2025 and

and super senior pensioners respectively. Out of 2588 grievances taken up, 1943 grievances

grievance resolution. The  balance cases have also been closed subsequent to the respective 
Pension Adalats through Inter-Ministerial review meetings. 
 
3.22. The Committee notes that Pension Adalats serve as an important institutional 
mechanism for expeditious and on -the-spot resolution of pension -related grievances. 
However, the effectiveness of such Adalats depends significantly on the extent to which 
pensioners are made aware of these opportunities in advance. The Committee is of the view 
that lack of timely and adequate dissemination of information may prevent many eligible 
pensioners, particularly those residing in remote areas or those with limited digital access, 
from availing themselves of this grievance redressal mechanism. 
 
3.23. The Committee emphasises the need for the Department to undertake 
widespread and well -coordinated awareness campaigns sufficiently in advance of 
organising Pension Adalats, so as to ensure that all pensioners with pending grievances 
are informed and able to participate. Information regarding Pension Adalats sho uld be 
disseminated through multiple channels, including pensioner welfare associations, 
pension disbursing banks, post offices, and relevant Government offices, in addition to 
digital platforms such as official websites, pension portals, SMS alerts, and social media.

VIII. Integration of Pension Processes 
End-to-end digitization of pension application process:  
3.28. A single simplified form (Form 6 -A) was introduced under Bhavishya 
replacing nine older forms. More than 42,000 retiring officials have filled their pension 
application through Form 6 -A. Continuous and dedicated efforts are being made with PFMS 
for achievi ng end -to-end digitization of pension application process by integrating PFMS 
with Bhavishya.  
 
3.29. The Committee notes that at present, retiring employees are required to obtain No 
Objection Certificates (NOCs) from multiple field offices and establishments w here they 
have served during their entire career. The Committee observes that this process requires 
retiring employees to approach various offices individually, often located in different 
geographical locations, which results in considerable inconvenience,  delays, and 
administrative hardship. The Committee is of the view that such a decentralised and manual 
clearance mechanism is not aligned with the Department‘s ongoing efforts towards 
digitisation of pension processing and retirement formalities. 
 
3.30. The Committee further observes that the Department has already taken significant 
steps towards digital transformation of pension processing through initiatives such as the 
Bhavishya portal and digital submission of pension -related documents. However, the proce ss 
of obtaining NOCs from multiple offices remains largely manual and fragmented. The 
Committee is of the considered view that continuation of such manual procedures undermines 
the objective of ensuring seamless, transparent, and timely settlement of retirement benefits. 
  

 
44 
3.31. The Committee recommends that the Department develop and implement a 
centralised digital clearance mechanism through a dedicated online portal, integrated 
with existing pension processing systems, to enable retiring employees to obtain al l 
required No Objection Certificates (NOCs) electronically. The portal should 
automatically route clearance requests to all concerned offices, provide real -time status 
tracking, and ensure electronic issuance of NOCs in a time-bound manner.  
 
3.32. The Committee is of the view that such a digital and centralised system would 
enhance transparency, improve administrative efficiency, prevent delays in settlement 
of retirement benefits, and significantly reduce hardship faced by retiring employees, 
while aligning with the Government’s objective of strengthening digital governance. 
 
Integration with Banks 
3.33. The Committee , upon examining  the written submission made by the Department,  
notes that integration of banks with the Bhavishya portal has been progressing with the 
addition of HDFC Bank, Indian Bank, and ICICI Bank in 2025, bringing the total number of 
integrated banks to nine. This development has successfully covered approximately 90  per 
cent of pensioners and family pensioners, facilitating smoother processing of pension -related 
services. However, the Committee observes that the remaining 10 per cent of pensioners are 
yet to be brought under this coverage. 
 
3.34. The Committee recommends that the Department expedite efforts to achieve 100 
per cent integration by onboarding the remaining banks at the earliest, ensuring 
comprehensive digital access to pension services for all beneficiaries.

Bankers’ Awareness Programs: 
3.35. Workshops were held to educate field bankers on pension rules and procedures.

disbursing banks. 
 
3.36. The Committee appreciates the awareness programmes initiated by the Department to 
educate pensioners about various pension -related services and processes.  The Committee is 
of the view that in view of the alarming increase in cyber frauds and online financial scams, 
retired Government employees and pensioners ha ve emerged as a particularly vulnerable 
group for such scamsters, especially in relation to pension payments, Digital Life Certificates, 
bank KYC, and Ponzi schemes or "loan" offers routed through phone calls, SMS, emails and 
social media. 
 
3.37. The Committee recommend that, in view of the alarming increase in cyber 
frauds and online financial scams, the Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare 
should design and implement targeted cyber -security and fraud -prevention awareness 
campaigns for Government pensi oners and family pensioners, in coordination with 
banks, India Post Payments Bank, Common Service Centres and Pensioners’ Welfare 
Associations, so as to sensitise them against sharing OTPs/passwords, how to identify 
and respond  to fake “pension verificatio n” calls or links, and to apprise them of

RECCOMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
 
Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances 
 
Budget Analysis of DARPG 
 
1. In order to improve budget utilisation and enhance the credibility of projections, 
the Committee recommends that the Department should undertake a rigorous internal 
review of its past three years’ schemes and activities, identifying specific heads and 
projects where slippages occurred and preparing realistic activity-wise timelines so that 
future BEs are based on clearly phased implementation plans rather than broad 
aggregate estimates.  
(Para 2.11) 
 
2. The Committee further recommends that the Department may strengthen its 
quarterly monitoring mechanism, with clearly defined physical and financial milestones 
and periodic mid-year reviews, so that emerging underspending is identified early and 
corrective measures such as re-appropriation within heads, timely re-allocation, or 
expediting pending approvals can be taken to minimise the gap between BE, RE and 
actual expenditure. 
(Para 2.12) 
 
3. The Committee also recommends that, while formulating projections for 
submission to the Ministry of Finance, the Department should base its proposals on 
demonstrable past utilisation, realistic assessment of implementation capacity and 
firmed-up project pipelines, so that the difference between projections and finally 
approved BEs, as well as subsequent revisions, is narrowed and the credibility of the 
Department’s budgetary demand is enhanced. 
(Para 2.13) 
 
4. In Committee’s view, persistent high under-utilisation across 28 heads despite 
the cash-management provisions issued by Ministry of Finance (Annexure-I)  indicates 
that the Department’s initial MEP/QEP and budget projections were not adequately 
aligned with realistic implementation capacity, and that mid-year adjustments and re-
appropriation were not effectively undertaken. 
(Para 2.17) 
 
5. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should undertake a 
detailed head-wise review, identify specific administrative, procedural or 
implementation bottlenecks and furnish a factual note explaining the reasons for 
non-utilisation in each case, together with corrective steps proposed, to the Committee. 
                           (Para 2.18) 
 
6. The Committee further recommends that from the subsequent years the 
Department should prepare its Budget Estimates and Monthly/Quarterly Expenditure 
Plans on the basis of a detailed assessment of each scheme, including the stage of 
preparation, tendering schedule and actual spending pattern in previous years, so that 

 
49 
expenditure is spread more evenly across the quarters, rush of spending at the end of 
the year can be avoided, and the Department’s budget proposals and cash-flow 
projections become more realistic and reliable within the existing cash-management 
system.                                              
           (Para 2.19) 
 
7. The Committee recommends that the Department may strengthen its internal 
project planning and procurement processes, particularly for components under the 
Comprehensive System for Redressal of Public Grievances, so that budgetary 
provisions translate into timely implementation and avoid recurring downward 
revisions at the Revised Estimates stage. 
(Para 2.23) 
 
Policies, Programmes and Schemes of DARPG 
 
8. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Department in conceptualizing 
and conducting the National Good Governance Webinar Series on diverse and relevant 
themes covering sectors such as Health, Education, Environment, Water Management, 
Sports, Public Grievances, Service Delivery and Innovation, among others. The 
Committee observes that these webinars have served as an effective platform for 
cross-learning and dissemination of best practices among various levels of 
administration. While commending the Department for this constructive endeavour, the 
Committee feels that certain emerging areas of governance, particularly those involving 
the application of advanced technologies, may also be included as recurring themes in 
order to enhance the scope and contemporary relevance of the Webinar Series. 
(Para 2.38) 
 
9. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while selecting themes for the 
National Good Governance Webinar Series, the Department should also include “Use of 
Artificial Intelligence for Improving Governance and Service Delivery” as a recurring 
theme, so that States and districts can learn how AI-based tools are being practically 
applied by award winning initiatives and can replicate these solutions to make 
governance simpler, faster and more citizen friendly. 
(Para 2.39) 
 
10. The Committee further wishes that a consolidated statement indicating how 
many of the best practices showcased in these events have been replicated by other 
States or Ministries, and what outcomes have been achieved thereby, may be furnished.  
(Para 2.40) 
 
11. The Committee proposes that the Department institute an award to Ministries 
and Departments/Institutions, under their purview, that demonstrate exemplary budget 
planning, measured inter alia by the minimum variance between Budget Estimates, 
Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure, so as to promote healthy competition and 
strengthen fiscal discipline across the Government.  
(Para 2.41) 
 

 
50 
12. The Committee observes that the number of public grievances registered has 
increases over the years. While this indicates a growing public awareness and 
confidence in the grievance redressal mechanism, the Committee is of the view that it is 
equally important to undertake root cause analysis of these complaints and assess the 
tangible outcomes arising therefrom. 
(Para 2.47) 
 
13. In view of this, the Committee recommends that the Department institutionalise 
comprehensive root cause analysis of recurring and high-impact grievances, and use the 
findings to drive systemic reforms aimed at reducing the incidence of complaints rather 
than merely improving disposal figures. The Committee further emphasises that 
grievance redressal should not be treated as a statistical exercise and that particular 
attention should be paid to unresolved and repeatedly reopened cases, with a focus on 
ensuring actual citizen satisfaction and meaningful resolution rather than mere formal 
closure. 
(Para 2.48)

(NeSDA) 2025 has been initiated and is expected to be completed by June/July 2026.           
In the written submission made by the Department, the Committee notes that delays 
and submission of incomplete data by certain Single Points of Contact (SPoCs) from 
States and Union Territories have been affecting the efficiency and accuracy of the 
assessment process. The Committee further notes that the Department has been 
organizing review meetings with the SPoCs and plans to hold workshops to sensitize 
and support them in ensuring timely and accurate submission of data and information, 
which is a welcome step.                  (Para 2.53) 
 
15. The Committee recommends that, as the National Conference on e-Governance 
already brings together senior State IT and administrative officers, DARPG and MeitY,

time-bound data-quality improvements.  
(Para 2.54)

implementing the District Good Governance Index (DGGI) as a progressive initiative 
towards benchmarking governance performance at the district level. The Committee 
notes that this innovative measure has introduced a spirit of healthy competition among 
districts and has provided a valuable framework for identifying gaps and promoting 
citizen-centric governance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that DGGI be 
expanded to more States, with particular attention to aspirational districts and those 
with high grievance loads, so that district-level competition and data-driven governance 
are strengthened where they are needed most. 
                                  (Para 2.60)
  

 
51

Functions of the Department 
 
1.4 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, functions of the 
Department are as under: 
 
i. Appointment, resignation and removal of the Chief Justice of India and Judges 
of the Supreme Court of India; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of 
absence (including leave allowance), pensions and travelling allowances; 
ii. Appointment, resignation and removal etc. of Chief Justice and Judges of 
High Courts in States; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence 
(including leave allowances), pensions and travelling allowances; 
iii. Appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial Officers in Union 
Territories; 
iv. Constitution and organization (excluding jurisdiction and powers) of the 
Supreme Court (but including contempt of such Court) and the fees taken 
therein; 
v. Constitution and organization of the High Courts and the Courts of Judicial 
Commissioners except provisions as to officers and servants of these Courts; 
vi. Administration of justice and constitution and organization of Courts in the 
Union Territories and fees taken in such Courts; 
vii. Courts fees and Stamp duties in the Union Territories; 
viii. Creation of All India Judicial Service; 
ix. Conditions of service of District Judges and other Members of Higher Judicial 
Service of Union Territories; 
x. Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory or exclusion 
of a Union Territory from the Jurisdiction of a High Court; 
xi. Legal Aid to the poor; 
xii. Administration of Justice; and 
xiii. Access to Justice, Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms.

1.18 In their written submission, the Department highlighted several problems affecting the 
implementation of the Scheme, including slow pace of expenditure, inadequate monitoring at 
the State level, procedural delays, delays in submission of e-payment files, law and order 
issues in certain States, limited working seasons, and challenges arising from the transition to 
the SNA-SPARSH model. 
1.19 During the course of examination of the Demands for Grants (DFG) for 2026–27, the 
Committee observed that many courts, especially High Courts and subordinate courts, do not 
have adequate basic facilities. The Committee noted that court buildings are often 
overcrowded and lack proper seating, sanitation, ventilation and other essential amenities for 
judges, lawyers and litigants. The Committee also observed that suitable facilities for women 
lawyers, including dedicated spaces and child-care or crèche facilities, are generally not 
available. In addition, the Committee noted shortcomings in digital infrastructure, such as 
poor internet connectivity and Wi-Fi facilities, which affect the effective functioning of e-
Courts. The Committee further observed that while better facilities are available in the 
Supreme Court of India, similar facilities have not been provided uniformly across High 
Courts and subordinate courts. 
1.20 The Committee notes that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for 
Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judiciary has played a significant role in 
augmenting judicial infrastructure across the States and Union Territories, as reflected 
in the cumulative release of Central assistance and the creation of Court halls and 
residential units. However, the Committee expresses concern over the slow pace of 
expenditure and utilisation of funds in several States during 2025–26, despite 
substantial releases made under the Scheme. 
1.21 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department in coordination 
with the State Governments and High Court Level Monitoring Committees, strengthen 
monitoring and review mechanisms to ensure timely utilisation of funds and completion 
of projects. The Committee also recommends that the Department take proactive 
measures to address procedural and system-related bottlenecks, including capacity 
building for effective implementation of the SNA-SPARSH framework, so that the 
objectives of the Scheme are achieved. 

 
12 
1.22 The Committee further recommends that the Department, in coordination with 
the judicial authorities and State Governments, take time-bound measures to upgrade 
court infrastructure across the country. The Committee emphasises the need for 
gender-sensitive court design, including provision of separate and adequate facilities for 
women lawyers, litigants and staff, as well as dedicated child-care and crèche facilities 
within court complexes. The Committee further recommends that deficiencies in digital 
infrastructure and the non-availability of proper network connectivity in courts be 
urgently addressed. The Committee also stress that such facilities should be uniformly 
extended to High Courts and subordinate courts, and not remain confined only to the 
Supreme Court of India.

1.21 The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 came into force with effect from 2nd October, 2009. 
The Act provides for the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas at intermediate Panchayat level 
for the purpose of providing access to justice to the citizens at their doorstep. In terms of 
Section 3(1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, State Governments, after consultation with the 
High Court concerned, may, by notification, establish one or two more Gram Nyayalayas for 
every Panchayat at intermediate level or a group of contiguous Panchayats at intermediate 
level in a district or where there is no Panchayat at intermediate level in any State, for a group 
of contiguous group Panchayats. Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas is, therefore, not 
mandatory on the part of State Governments as per the Act. However, the State Governments 
are requested from time to time to establish Gram Nyayalayas. Till date 488 Gram 
Nyayalayas have been notified by 15 States, out of which 334 Gram Nyayalayas are 
functional in 11 States as on 31.12.2025. 
 

 
13

Gram Nyayalayas which include ₹ 18.00 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya towards cost of 
establishing the Gram Nyayalaya as a one-time assistance and ₹ 3.20 lakh per Gram 
Nyayalaya per annum as recurring expenditure for a period of three years.  Till date, a sum of 
₹ 93.40 crore has been released under the Scheme of Gram Nyayalayas. The Gram 
Nyayalayas Scheme is now a sub-scheme of the CSS for development of Judicial 
Infrastructure.

26, new Gram Nyayalayas have been set up in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and the financial

under the Gram Nyayalaya component of the Scheme is expected to be fully utilised during 
the current financial year.   
1.26 The Department in their written submission made stated that it took note of several 
challenges faced in the implementation of the Scheme, including the non-mandatory nature of 
their establishment by States, the functioning of Gram Nyayalayas for only two days a week, 
inadequate infrastructure and ICT support, shortage of judicial officers and supporting staff, 
non-functional Mobile Courts in certain areas, lack of trained Nyayadhikaris, overlapping 
jurisdiction with regular Courts, and limited cooperation from the police and other State 
functionaries. 
1.27 The Committee is of the opinion that Gram Nyayalayas were intended to 
improve access to justice at the grassroots level. By establishing it, it will be able to 
provide speedy, affordable and decentralised justice, especially in rural and remote 
areas. Moreover, the success of Gram Nyayalayas depends on their regular functioning, 
availability of basic infrastructure, presence of trained judicial officers and adequate 
support from the State Governments. 

 
15 
1.28 The Committee observes that since establishment of Gram Nyayalayas is not 
mandatory for States and that, in many States where such Courts exist, they function 
only for two days a week, it restrict the effectiveness in disposal of cases. 
1.29 The  Committee in its 147th Report had recommended  that Gram Nyayalayas 
should function on all working days instead of one or two days a week, the Department 
stated that although the matter falls within the jurisdiction of the State Governments, 
the Department has issued a letter dated 30.04.2025 to the States regarding it. The 
Committee, however, reiterates its recommendation made in 147th Report that Gram 
Nyayalayas must function on all working days in order to effectively reduce the backlog 
of cases at the local level. The Committee believe that early creation of posts and timely 
filling up of vacancies of Nyayadhikaris would ensure uninterrupted functioning of 
Gram Nyayalayas.

1.30 This Project is being implemented by the Department under the guidance of e-
Committee, Supreme Court of India primarily for universal computerization of all District

1.31 Phase II of the e-Courts Project was implemented with a total outlay of ₹1,670 crore, 
against which an amount of ₹1,668.43 crore has been utilised. Phase II primarily focused on 
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) enablement of district and subordinate 
Courts during the period 2015–2023. Under this phase, 3,452 Court complexes and 18,735 
Courtrooms were computerised, wide area network (WAN) connectivity was established 
across Courts, and digital case management tools such as the National Judicial Data Grid 
(NJDG) were implemented. 

 
16 
1.32 Phase III of the e-Courts Project, with a total financial outlay of ₹7,210 crore spread 
over four years, was approved by the Cabinet on 13.09.2023. The objective of Phase III is to 
further enhance the use of technology in the judiciary to improve efficiency, transparency, 
and accessibility of justice. Building upon the achievements of Phase II, Phase III aims to 
strengthen digital case management systems, expand virtual Court facilities, and promote the 
use of Artificial Intelligence–based tools for legal research and judicial assistance. 
1.33 Under Phase III, an amount of ₹825 crore was allocated during 2023–24, against 
which an expenditure of ₹768.25 crore was incurred within a period of five months. During

achievements of Phase-III of e Courts Mission Mode Project as under:  
  
 The Wide Area Network (WAN) project is aimed at connecting all the District and

 Through the National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) litigants can access case information 
and more than 34.56 crore orders/judgments. 
 29 Virtual Courts have been set up in 21 States/UTs to try traffic offences. Over 9.54 
crore cases have been handled by these virtual Courts and in more than 90 lakhs

 Through Video conferencing, District & Subordinate Courts heard 
2,92,04,596 cases while the High Courts heard 97,33,584  cases (totaling 3.89

1.34 The Committee appreciates the significant progress made under the e-Courts 
Mission Mode Project by the Department under the guidance of the e-Committee, 
Supreme Court of India in strengthening digital infrastructure and enhancing access to 
justice. The Committee recommends that the remaining Court complexes under the 
WAN project be connected expeditiously and adequate cyber-security and system

1.35 The Committee notes that against the release of ₹931.08 crore under the Revised

1.46 The Department is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for the 
establishment of Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) for expeditious disposal of cases relating 
to rape and offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. 
The Scheme was introduced in October, 2019 pursuant to the enactment of the Criminal Law 
(Amendment) Act, 2018 and in compliance with the directions of the Supreme Court of India 
in Suo Motu Writ (Criminal) No. 1 of 2019. The Scheme has been extended on two occasions, 
with the latest extension up to 31.03.2026, at a total outlay of ₹1,952.23 crore, including a 
Central share of ₹1,207.24 crore to be met from the Nirbhaya Fund, for establishment of 790 
Fast Track Special Courts. However, in view of the current allocation of ₹200 crore for FY 
2025–26 and since the proposal for further extension of the Scheme is under consideration, 
an equivalent amount has been proposed under the Budget Estimates (BE) for FY 2026–27. 
1.47 At the inception of the Scheme, allocation of FTSCs was determined on the basis of 
pendency, with the criterion of one FTSC for every 65 to 165 pending cases. Based on this 
criterion, 31 States/Union Territories were initially found eligible to participate in the 
Scheme. However, Arunachal Pradesh opted out citing a very low number of pending cases 
under rape and POCSO categories. The Union Territory of Puducherry joined the Scheme at 
a later stage upon special request and operationalised an exclusive POCSO Court in May, 
2023. The Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has conveyed its willingness to 
join the Scheme but has not yet operationalised any FTSC. Further, the State of Jharkhand 
has decided to exit the Scheme vide letter dated 07.07.2025. Consequently, the Scheme is 
presently being implemented in 29 States/UTs. 
1.48 As per data furnished by the High Courts, as on 30.11.2025, a total of 774 FTSCs, 
including 398 exclusive POCSO Courts, are functional across 29 States/UTs. Since inception

VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT  
 
1.52 Despite its establishment as an independent Department on 1st January, 2010, it 
continues to be staffed from the common cadre of the Ministry of Home Affairs, with matters 
relating to recruitment and vacancies being handled in coordination with the Department of 
Personnel and Training. 

 
23 
1.53 The Committee notes that against a sanctioned strength of 102 posts, only 63 are 
presently in position in the Department, resulting in vacancies of about 39 per cent, 
which adversely affects its overall functioning. The Committee, in its earlier Reports, 
had expressed concern over the continued dependence of the Department on the 
Ministry of Home Affairs for meeting all its manpower requirements and had 
recommended the establishment of a separate cadre unit for the Department. The 
Committee reiterates the same. 
 
1.53 The Department informed that it has submitted a proposal to the Department of 
Personnel and Training and the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking bifurcation of the common 
cadre and full autonomy in personnel management. A separate proposal has also been sent to 
the Department of Expenditure for allocation of additional manpower to enable independent 
and smooth functioning of the Department. 
1.54 The Department also informed that the Ministry of Home Affairs has conveyed its 
‘No Objection’ for delinking the CSS/CSSS/CSCS cadre from MHA; however, it has 
expressed its inability to spare administrative staff owing to acute shortages across its sub-
cadres and has advised the Department of Justice to pursue the matter further with DoPT. 
Accordingly, the Department has taken up the issue with DoPT and requested expeditious 
consideration. DoPT convened a meeting with MHA and the Department of Justice on 9 
January 2026 and has sought additional information, which is being furnished by the 
Department in consultation with MHA. 
1.55 The Committee is of the view that shortage of staff strength hampers the smooth 
functioning of the Department.  While appreciating the steps taken by the Department 
to bridge this gap, the Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the 
matter of filling up vacancy with DoPT expeditiously and pursue the matter at the 
highest level to ensure early approval and implementation of an independent cadre, 
with clearly defined timelines, so as to address persistent manpower shortages and 
ensure smooth functioning of the Department.

CHAPTER-II 
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY 
 
2.0 Article 39A of the Constitution of India provides for free legal aid to the poor and 
weaker sections of the society and ensures justice for all. Also, Articles 14 and 22 (1) of the 
Constitution also make it obligatory for the State to ensure equality before law and a legal 
system which promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity to all. In this background, 
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted by the Parliament, which came into 
force on 9th November, 1995 to establish a nationwide network for providing free and 
competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society on the basis of equal 
opportunity. 
 
2.1 The NALSA monitors and evaluates implementation of legal aid programmes and 
lays down policies and principles for making legal services available under the Act. In every 
State, a State Legal Services Authority and in every High Court, a High Court Legal Services 
Committee has been constituted. District Legal Services Authorities, Taluk Legal Services 
Committees have been constituted in the Districts and most of the Taluks, respectively, to 
give effect to the policies and directions of the NALSA and to provide free legal services to 
the people and conduct Lok Adalats in the State. Supreme Court Legal Services Committee 
has been constituted to administer and implement the legal services programme insofar as it 
relates to the Supreme Court of India.
