Reduced expenditure at RE stage
6.0 In the detailed explanatory note furnished by the Ministry, it has been stated that for the year
2009-10, Plan allocation for the scheme “Propagation of Right to Information Act”  was reduced
from Rs. 14.16 crore to Rs. 10.66 crore in RE 2009-10 due to slow pace of expenditure, non-receipt
of Utilization Certificates from some State Governments, etc. and that unutilized surplus funds of
Rs. 0.35 crore could not be surrendered in time leading to lapse of funds. For the year 2010-11, Plan
allocation for the scheme “Propagation of Right to Information Act” was reduced from Rs. 19 crore

10
to Rs. 11.35 crore in RE 2010-11 due to slow pace of expenditure, non-receipt of Utilization
Certificates from some State Governments etc. In 2011-12, Plan allocation for the scheme “Propagation
of Right to Information Act” was reduced from Rs. 51.60 crore to Rs. 24.60 crore in RE 2011-12
due to slow pace of expenditure, non-receipt of Utilization Certificates from some State Governments
etc. The Committee noted that every year due to slow pace of expenditure and non receipt of
utilization certificate, the allocation was reduced at RE stage.
6.1 It has been stated that in 2009-10, the Plan allocation for “Plan Scheme for Administrative
Reforms” was reduced from Rs. 24 crore to Rs. 20 crore in RE 2009-10 due to slow pace of
expenditure in the first 6 months. For the year 2010-11, the allocation for “Plan Scheme for
Administrative Reforms” was reduced from Rs. 27.50 crore to Rs. 22.50 crore in RE 2010-11 due
to slow pace of expenditure in the first 6 months. For 2011-12, the allocation for “Plan Scheme for
Administrative Reforms” was reduced from Rs. 20.11 crore to Rs. 17.00 crore in RE 2011-12 due
to slow pace of expenditure in the first 6 months. The Committee noted that BE for the years 2009-10
to 2011-12 was reduced at RE stage due to slow pace of expenditure in first 6 months.
6.2 The Ministry has  stated that in 2009-10, the provision for the Plan scheme “Pensioners’
Portal” was reduced from Rs. 0.50 crore to Rs. 0.18 crore in RE 2009-10 due to delay in
commencement of some activities under the scheme. For the year 2010-11, the provision for the Plan
scheme “Pensioners’ Portal” was reduced from Rs. 0.50 crore to Rs. 0.35 crore in RE 2010-11 due
to delay in commencement of some activities under the scheme, non-receipt of Utilization Certificates
etc. In 2011-12, the provision for the Plan scheme “Pensioners’ Portal” was made Rs. 0.42 crore in
BE and RE 2011-12. Anticipated saving of Rs. 0.05 crore is mainly due to non-submission of utilization
certificates by a few Pensioners Associations and delay in commencement of some activities under the
scheme. Here also, the Committee noted that the allocations were reduced at RE stage for single
reason i.e. non receipt of utilization certificate.
6.3 The Committee is constrained to note the low level of expenditure/non-expenditure of
various Plan funds due to non-finalization of schemes/delay in implementation of various
schemes. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the reasons furnished by the
Ministry for reducing the expenditure at the RE stage, under the above mentioned vital Plan
Schemes for the last three years, have remained almost the same. The Committee wonders
why this trend was not noticed and arrested by taking appropriate remedial steps. The
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that such causes, when once identified, should have
been carefully evaluated and remedial steps should have been taken in anticipation so that
they did not recur. The Committee is of the considered view that since the Ministry is a
crucial agency dealing with the human resources of the Government and other important
Central Policies/Schemes, optimum utilization of available funds should be ensured, or
otherwise, reductions at the RE stage in this manner  can be seen as a reflection on the
efficiency of the Ministry.
6.4 In this context, the Committee also took note of the deposition of the representative of DoPT
that there was provision for augmentation of training facilities for the ISTM and that due to non-
submission of schemes by the CPWD in time, Rs. 10 crores which was kept for that purpose was
reduced at the RE level.
6.5 The Committee recommends that such laches should be avoided to the extent possible,
and that steps should be taken in advance to ensure that such delays do not impede
development and modernization. The Committee is of the view that agencies and individuals
should be made accountable for such delays.
6.6 During the course of deposition before it, the Committee was also apprised that out of the Plan
allocation of Rs. 2 crore for the new Plan scheme “IT enabling of core CVC Processes”, the Central

11
Vigilance Commission could utilize only Rs. 0.83 crore in 2009-10 due to the failure of Tata

6.7 The Committee is of the considered opinion that when funds were made available to the
organization so liberally for the purpose of engaging consultants, the latter should have shown
matching degree of enthusiasm and initiative to see that the activities for which funds were
provided were accomplished. The Committee feels that periodic evaluation by the Ministry of
the progress of such schemes can go a long way in avoiding such happenings.
6.8 The Committee further notes that in 2010-11, the allocation for the Plan scheme “CBI
e-Governance” was reduced from Rs. 8 crore to Rs. 0.10 crore in RE 2010-11 due to delay in
finalizing/obtaining approval for the activities under the scheme.
6.9 It has also been stated that in 2010-11, a fresh allocation of Rs. 3.89 Crore has been provided
for the new Plan scheme “Technical and Forensic Support Units” of CBI during 2010-11 of which
CBI could utilize only around Rs. 0.60 crore.
6.10 For the year 2011-12, the allocation of Rs. 0.01 crore provided for the Plan scheme “Technical
and Forensic Support Units” of CBI during 2011-12 has been enhanced to Rs. 3.32 crore in RE 2011-
12 out of which CBI could utilize only around Rs. 2.63 crore towards the cost of vehicles, items
purchased for TAFSU, etc.
6.11 The Committee feels that CBI, being a premier agency, should have well thought out
proposals and realistic plan of action regarding utilization of funds, more particularly the Plan
funds, which are imperative for growth and development, so that such non-utilisation/under-
utilisation do not occur in future.

following the Government’s deliberations with the Joint Drafting Committee.  The said Bill was
referred to this Committee by Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha in consultation with the Hon’ble
Chairman, Rajya Sabha and the Committee made an in depth examination of the Bill.
Extensive deliberations took place covering a very wide range of stakeholders and thereafter,
the Committee presented an exhaustive Report (48
th Report) on the Bill to both the Houses of
Parliament on the 9 th December, 2011. The Committee finds that the Lokpal and the Lokayaktas
Bill, 2011 introduced in Lok Sabha on the 22 nd December, 2011 contain many of the suggestions
made by this Committee. It may be mentioned that the Committee, in its Report, had very
strongly suggested for the Constitutional status for Lokpal and Lokayuktas. The Committee
hopes that the Ministry would take adequate precaution in future to see that the Annual
Report gives a complete account of developments/happenings of the relevant period.

IMPLEMENTATION OF THE RTI ACT
17.0. The Committee takes note of the following initiatives made by the Ministry:–
(a) RTI Anthem:
In order to create awareness on RTI, an RTI anthem has been launched on 15
th August,
2011 which was telecast and broadcast through radio, television and theatre throughout
the country and in eleven languages.
(b) RTI Fellowship:
RTI fellowships were awarded to four fellows from the field of civil society and media.
17.1 The Committee takes note of the Ministry’s reply that under the Centrally-sponsored Schemes,
over 31,000 SPIOs and AAs were trained at district levels in States and 500 CPIOs and AAs were
trained from the Central Ministries/Departments. Two trainings were organized at the National Law
School of India University, Bangalore for Chief Information Commissioners and Information

15
Commissioners from the States. The online-certificate course on RTI has been continued and is
running successfully.
17.2 The Committee notes from the reply furnished by the Ministry that the independent Study
commissioned in 2008, to understand the key issues and constraints in effectively implementing the
RTI Act found that the PIOs in majority of cases were least sensitized to look after the demands
of the people, particularly those from the marginalized and ignorant sections of the society.
Importantly, the study observed that 75% of the people were dissatisfied with the quality of
information they received and the cause for this was found to be the lack of will to shift from
“culture of reluctant response” to a “culture of complete openness”. In this regard, the study
recommended that in order to facilitate citizens in filing RTI requests/appeals alternate channels like
common service centres, post offices and RTI portal should be utilized. The appropriate Government
may amend the rules so as to facilitate ease in paying the requisite fees from any part of the
country, as per Section 6(1).
17.3 The Committee recommends that the suggestions made in the Study should be given
proper thought and consideration, particularly those relating to sensitization of PIOs and
speedier disposal. The Ministry’s scheme for training of PIOs, may be a good step. It is also vital
that the recommendations made in the Study are followed through, till their logical conclusion.
17.4 The Committee feels that measures such as effective training of PIOs, publicity
campaigns, more proactive disclosure, better record management and more infrastructure for
public authorities are extremely important to ensure that the maximum benefit of the RTI Act
accrue to the public.
17.5 The Committee further takes note of the suggestion made in the Study that e-Hearing
of cases may be adopted for speedy disposal. The Committee takes cognizance of the
recommendation made in the Study that third party audits should be commissioned by the
Information Commissions to empanelled civil society organizations.
17.6 With regard to achieving the objective of the RTI Act, the Committee is of the
considered view that much of it depends upon the proper implementation of the provisions of
Section 4 of the Act relating to proactive disclosur es. The RTI Act casts an obligation on every
Public Authority to provide as much information in the public domain on an ongoing basis so
that public have minimum resort to the use of this Act for obtaining information. The
Committee feels that quite a lot needs to be done in so far as implementation of the provisions
of Section 4(2) of the RTI Act is concerned. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the
Ministry should come out with a specific and time bound programme whereunder, the various
Public Authorities should examine threadbare what all information available with them or
generated in the course of their functioning should be placed in public domain. Further, in
order to ensure that the said programme progresses as per schedule, the Ministry should also
provide for monitoring of the action taken by various Public Authorities in compliance of the
said provisions of the RTI Act. The Committee feels that once this initial exercise is undertaken,
it would not be burdensome for the Public Authorities to update/add to the said information
on an ongoing basis.
OVERSTAY WHILE ON DEPUTATION
18.0 The Ministry, in its Annual Report, has stated that this Department has reiterated decisions
taken on 17
th June, 2010 and on 20 th November, 2006, that it will be the responsibility of the immediate
superior officer to ensure that the deputationist does not overstay. In the event of the officer
overstaying for any reason whatsoever, he/she is liable to disciplinary action and other adverse
consequences which would include the period of unauthorised overstay not being counted for service

16
for the purpose of pension and that any increment due during the period of unauthorized overstay
being deferred with cumulative effect, till the date on which the officer rejoins his parent cadre. All
Ministries/Departments have been advised that henceforth no ex-post facto approval for regularization
of overstay on deputation would be allowed.
18.1 The Committee feels that deputation, as a policy, has been envisaged to facilitate
mobility of personnel between Departments so that the concerned person as well as the
Department(s) benefit from the process. When the person on deputation reverts to his parent
Department, he can put to use the innovative practices that he imbibed from the other
Department and also, the latter can derive benefits from the processes followed in the person’s
parent Department. Therefore, once the period of deputation is over, it is beyond reason that
the person overstays. The Committee is of the considered view that the existing tendency of
treating deputation as a tool by persons considering certain places uncomfortable, to ensure
posting in a better place, or to get a hometown posting, should be discouraged. The Committee
hopes that the abovementioned step taken by the Ministry would help in curbing such
tendencies.
18.2 The Committee in this context further observes that there are umpteen instances of
Government officials remaining on deputation for years together, moving from one department
of Government to another and even to other statutory/autonomous organizations and their stay
in their parent organization remains very limited. The Committee is of the considered view
that the instrument of deputation does serve public interest only if the deputations take place
in departments/organizations where the qualification and work experience of the deputationist
officer are relevant and secondly the deputation continues for a reasonable period within which
the borrowing department/organization is able to benefit from the experience/exposure of the
deputationist officer. When deputations take place and continue in violation of these conditions,
the Committee feels that, in such cases, the instrument of deputation is being misused for
personal gain by the deputationist officer. Such tendencies need to be curbed with a strong
hand. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has issued strict guidelines against
unauthorized overstay while on deputation. The Committee in this context feels that the
instructions issued by the Ministry may be made applicable on the lending Government
departments from where Government officials go on deputation to different statutory/autonomous
bodies of Government of India. Such an action, the Committee feels would be able to regulate
and conform the deputation of all Government officials to the desired objective.

25.0 The Committee noted that providing better opportunities of excellent career advancement
with the objectives to retain and maintain the spirit of excellence of public service for effective
and efficient delivery is one of the missions of the Department of Personnel & Training. For
the accomplishment of this mission, it becomes imperative on the part of the DoPT to ensure
that there are in place, well laid down rules/procedures/guidelines for the purpose of regulating
recruitment as well as promotions in the different Services under the Government of India
which are under the control and supervision of the DoPT.
25.1 The Committee notes that the DoPT is the cadre management authority in respect of the
I.A.S., the Central Secretariat Services and the Group A Services. The Committee impresses
upon the DoPT to lay down sound basic principles in the matter of recruitment and promotions
for the guidance of the attached subordinate offices of the Government of India and the various
autonomous statutory bodies, where the human resource employed/hired is being paid from the
Government exchequer. Such an action, the Committee feels, would be in consonance with the
role and function of the DoPT namely, laying down HR strategy and policy for the Government
of India and advising the Ministries/Departments in the implementation of the same.
26.0 The Committee during the course of the oral evidence of the Secretary, DoPT on 17
th April,
2012 learnt that the strength of work force in Government in the country is the lowest i.e., 0.5%
as compared to the overall position in other countries in whose case the figure stands somewhere near
1.5%. The Committee was told that the reduction in the workforce in the Government sector is
basically the result of the economy drives undertaken in the country.

20
26.1 The Committee, however, does not see this reduction in the workforce in the Government
sector as a healthy trend. In Committee’s view, such a trend can have major negative
implications, compared to the meagre benefits of savings on account of putting in place a
leaner administration. The Committee further feels that the shortage of workforce is being
felt evenly in the various Government establishments leading to engagement of workforce on
contract basis and also outsourcing some of its activities. This also includes engaging of retired
Government officials in all types of Government establishments. The Committee does not see
this to be a healthy trend because the level of accountability of these contract appointees is
definitely lesser than regular appointees in Government. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that the DoPT may ascertain the magnitude of re-employment/contractual
employment in all types of Government establishments falling under their mandate and find
out ways and means to ensure that their sanctioned strength matches their manpower
requirement and the posts are filled up in terms of the recruitment rules rather than on an
ad-hoc basis through contract/re-employment.
26.2 In this context, the Committee also learnt about delay in the filling up of vacancies in the
grades of US/DS in the CSS due to certain litigation on the issue of seniority between the Direct
Recruit and the Promotee.
26.3 The Committee is unhappy to note that the issue of seniority between DRs and
Promotees in the CSS is still under litigation even after indulgence of the DoPT for well over
a decade. The Committee would like the DoPT to proactively and resolutely intervene for a
solution that is just and fair and takes care of legitimate concerns of both the DRs and the
Promotees.

CHAPTER-IV
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
29.0 UPSC is a constitutional body responsible for conducting examination for appointment to the
higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government including recruitment to the All India
Services. UPSC is created under Article 315 of the Constitution of India. The Commission’s charter
of duties is given in Articles 320 and 321 of the Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the Commission
to conduct examinations for appointments to services of the Union and to advise Central Government
on all matters relating to framing of recruitment rules, method of recruitment and the principles to be
followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to another. There is a provision for
consulting the Commission on matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed
in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and on disciplinary matters. Article
322 of the Constitution envisages, inter-alia, that the expenses of the UPSC including salaries,
allowances and pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall be ‘ charged’ on the
Consolidated Fund of India.
29.1 The Committee, while examining the Grants, had an opportunity to peruse the Annual Report
of UPSC. The Committee took note of the following initiatives/steps taken by the Commission:
(i) ONLINE RECEIVING OF APPLICATION
29.2 The Committee noted from the Annual Report of UPSC that 100% online mode for submission
of applications has been introduced for Engineering Services Examination, 2011, Combined Defence
Services-II Examination, 2011 and Central Police Forces (AC) Examination, 2011 except for the
applicants of specific remote areas, for whom offline application mode was also allowed. The
feasibility of introducing 100% online mode for submission of applications in other UPSC Examinations
is under consideration in the Commission.
29.3 The Committee appreciates the step taken by UPSC which is beneficial to candidates.
The Committee hopes that this would cut short the overall time taken in the conduct of the
examination.
(ii) IN SER VICE TRAINING OF CANDIDATES FROM RESERVED CATEGORIES
29.4 The Committee notes that UPSC recommended in-service training to 24 candidates belonging
to the Scheduled Castes, 11 to the Scheduled Tribes and 45 to the Other Backward Classes who were
selected for appointment on the basis of relaxed standards so that they could come up to the general
standard. Duration of in-service training ranged from three months to one year after their appointment
to the post in the areas comprising the duties attached to the post.
(iii) DELAY IN SENDING OFFERS OF APPOINTMENT
29.5 The UPSC, in its Annual Report, has expressed a firm view that candidates recommended by
it should not be made to wait for years for the receipt of the offers of appointment from the concerned
Ministries. It is also noted in this respect that in many cases, candidates selected by the Commission,
in the meantime, secure placement elsewhere and do not become available for appointment under the
Government thus rendering the whole exercise of selection of such candidates futile and infructuous.

24
29.6 The Committee is happy to note that UPSC has taken cognizance of this week area in
Government’s functioning. The Committee recommends that the concerned Ministries should
take serious note of such delays and that they should devise appropriate measures to ensure
that candidates recommended by UPSC, are issued offers of appointment, without delay.
(iv) DELAY IN NOTIFICATION OF RECRUITMENT RULES
29.7 The Committee could gather from the Annual Report that there is delay on the part of
Ministries/Departments in notification of Recruitment Rules.
29.8 The Committee is of the view that such delay in notification hinders the recruitment
process and therefore, desires that the Ministries/Departments should take due care and
caution to make sure that such delays do not occur. Absence of Recruitment Rules eventually
pave way for ad hoc actions and mal-exercise of discretion which are totally undesirable. The
Committee recommends pro-active action on the part of the Ministry in this very important
area.

29.9 The Committee noted that UPSC has, as a pilot project, successfully conducted an on-line test
for recruitment to certain posts, in order to shortlist about 4000 candidates, who had applied for the

CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
30.0 CBI is entrusted with the investigation and prosecution in corruption cases against public
servants, private persons, firms and other cases of serious crimes.
(i) V ACANCIES IN CBI
30.1. According to the Annual Report of CBI (para 6.1.1), the total sanctioned strength of CBI as
on December 31, 2011 was 6590 against which 5666 officers were in position with 924 posts lying
vacant. The vacancies existed in the ranks of Special/Additional Director
 (2), Joint Director (1),
Deputy Inspector-General of Police (3), Superintendent of Police (34), Additional Superintendent of
Police (9), Deputy Superintendent of Police (133), Inspector (183), Sub-Inspector (143), Assistant
Sub-Inspector (16), Head Constable (21) and Constable (124). The posts of 89 Law Officers and
40 Technical Officers at various levels, were also lying vacant.
30.2. In its reply furnished to the questionnaire, the Ministry has stated the position as under:–

When enquired about vacancies in CBI, the Committee was apprised of the  following reasons:
• CBI is not getting officers from the CPOs/State Governments on deputation as these
organisations are expanding and are unable to spare officials for CBI.
• Officers of some States are getting higher pay scales than CBI and hence are not entitled
for deputation to CBI as per existing RRs.
• Pay package in some other organizations and States are better than CBI and hence the
officers are not willing to join CBI.
• Limited number of candidates are selected on deputation in CBI due to very high
standards of selection process/eligibility criteria fixed. Moreover, not many candidates
fulfill the minimum requirements.
• Filling up of vacancies under Direct Recruitment Quota is a lengthy process.
• Action is being taken to hold DPCs for promotion of the personnel in the promotion
quota.
• Non-availability of eligible SC/ST candidates.
• Officials in the feeder grade are not eligible for promotion as per the existing Recruitment
Rules.
• Recruitment Rules are not yet finalized.
30.3 Similarly, the Committee could gather from CBI’s Annual Report that the sanctioned strength
of Directorate of Prosecution is 318 against which 229 personnel are in position with 89 posts lying
vacant.
30.4 The Ministry, in its reply to the questionnaire, stated:–
The Government had approved filling up of 60 posts of Special/Assistant Special
Prosecutor in CBI on contract basis. Selection process was carried out all over the country to
fill up all the 60 posts. However only 50 suitable candidates could be selected. Of these, 47
candidates joined and 03 officials refused to join. Out of 47 candidates who joined, (08) have
resigned subsequently.
30.5 The Committee is given to understand that by and large, CBI cases are conducted by its own
prosecutors in the courts. In High Courts, suitable and competent Advocates are engaged as CBI
Retainer Counsels with the approval of DoPT/Ministry of Law to represent CBI. Keeping in view the
large number of vacancies of CBI, Law Officers and resultant growing number of cases pending trial
in various courts, including the newly-created Special Courts, the Government of India has introduced

26
a scheme for appointment of Special Prosecutor in CBI on contract basis for a period of one year
extendable upto three years as a stopgap arrangement.
30.6 The Committee would like to place on record its deep anguish  over the vacancies
existing in CBI at various levels. The Committee is perturbed to note that inspite of its
repeated recommendations on this issue, in its various Reports on Demands for Grants of the
Ministry of Personnel and its 24
th Report on “Working of CBI”, the situation, instead of
improving, has progressively worsened.
30.7 The Committee fails to understand how, the country’s premier investigating agency,
whose mandate has witnessed an unprecedented increase in the recent years, can be expected
to function efficiently and keep up with the high expectations placed on it by the public, judiciary
and legislature, with such a large shortfall of manpower on several important posts. The situation
is beyond justification because in the proposed Lokpal regime, the role of CBI in investigating
corruption cases is bound to expand  tremendously. Therefore, CBI can ill afford to have such
large number of vacancies. The Committee strongly feels it to be a matter of serious concern
that the officers and staff of CBI, who are already under immense stress and strain, will surely
not be able to keep pace with the workload, if the vacancies continue to exist.
30.8 The Committee strongly recommends that strategic steps should be taken on a war
footing, with strict deadlines fixed and the Ministry, in co-ordination with CBI, should devise
measures to fill up these vacancies. Also, measures should be adopted in a planned manner,
to create a conducive working environment so that new talent is attracted to join the
organization. The Committee desires that it should be apprised of the steps taken in this
regard, in the Action taken reply.
(ii) DEPENDENCE ON THE OFFICERS ON DEPUTATION
30.9 The Committee, in its 24
th Report on “Working of CBI”, had recommended that much less
dependence should be placed on deputation. However, the Ministry, in its Action taken reply, had stated
that:
Induction of officers on deputation from outside the CBI brings in the experience and much
wider exposure in dealing with investigation of various kinds of complex crimes. Induction of
these officers also improves the coordination and interaction with the State Police, which is
important for successful investigation of cases.
In its Action Taken Report (41
st Report), the Committee has further reiterated its recommendations
and directed the Ministry to reconsider and inform the Committee of the outcome in this regard.
30.10 Now, the Ministry, in its Action taken note, has stated that:
The Officers joining CBI on deputation with experience of working in State Police have much
wider exposure in dealing with the investigation of various kinds of crime as compared to the
officers of the CBI. Taking officers from State Police also improves the coordination and
interaction with the States, whose consent is mandatory for taking up any investigation by the
CBI. If CBI is to be made Premier Investigation Agency, the officers from States Police must
be taken on deputation so that the States also have confidence in the functioning of the
Agency as their officers are working in the organization. Any dilution in this regard will give
rise to the suspicion of branding CBI as Agency of Central Government and also may lead
to withholding of consent under DSPE Act by the State Governments.
30.11 The Committee does not find merit in the argument put forward that if officers from
States’ Police are not taken on deputation in CBI, this will give rise to the suspicion of

27
branding CBI as agency of Central Government and also may lead to withholding of consent
under DSPE Act by the State Governments. The Committee does not find any logic in such
an argument. The act of giving consent by the State for investigation into a case depends on
the nature of the crime, gravity of the offence, etc. The Committee fails to understand how
the presence of deputationists in CBI, is in any way, likely to improve the decision making
process in this regard.
30.12 The Committee strongly feels that the good reputation that CBI currently enjoys due
to its pretty reasonable conviction rate, can also be attributed to the commendable way in
which departmental officers, whose skills have been honed to deal with specialized and
complicated crimes, owing to their continuous exposure to such  cases, have ensured successful
investigation and prosecution.
30.13 The Committee  took note of the reply furnished by the Ministry that over the years, need
was felt to have a small core group of officers for the sake of continuity but by no means it was
intended to convert the deputationist character of the CBI into a non-deputationist one.
30.14 The Committee strongly feels that this submission is beyond justification. It is of the
considered view that investigation skills that are expected from an officer of CBI are inherently
different from those expected from a  police officer posted in the States. The very fact that,
when the State police fails to solve a case, it is referred to CBI, suggests that the skills
expected of a CBI officer are different and specialized. Therefore, the Committee strongly
recommends that the departmental officers in CBI should form and continue to form the
backbone of the organisation and that any attempt to dilute their strength should be strongly
discouraged and resisted.
30.15 The Committee is of the view that by giving sufficient training and exposure to the
departmental officers in various fields, they will, over a period of time, evolve into experts in
such fields. So, greater emphasis should be given to steps such as skill enhancement of the
CBI departmental personnel, rather than encouraging deputation. Induction of deputationists
in CBI should be strictly on a selective and merit basis aimed to instill talent and skill in the
organization and it should not be a routine exercise of filling up deputation quota from the
States.
30.16 A lso, the Committee cannot ignore the observation made by the  Committee set up in CBI to
study the “Empowerment of the Investigating Officer” in 2005 that “there appears to be an unspoken
and underlying grouse with the direct CBI officers regarding the absorption of deputationists and fixing
of their seniority vis-à-vis the absorbed officers. There have been instances where very junior deputationists
with hardly 10 years of service, on absorption were promoted as Additional Supdt. of Police in the CBI.
On the other hand the direct recruits of CBI continue to stagnate at much lower ranks”.
30.17 The Committee is of the considered view that in order to attract fresh talent, a
conducive working environment and adequate promotional prospects are vital factors. The
Committee feels that in order to ensure a satisfactory working environment, the departmental
officers of CBI should be actively involved in the medium and long term decision policy
making processes in CBI so that they are adequately groomed to hold higher responsibilities.
The Committee would also like to emphasize the dire need of protecting the promotional
interests of the departmental officers in CBI and recommends that steps should be taken to
avoid stagnation at various levels where posts are manned by departmental officers.
(iii) RE-EMPLOYMENT OF RETIRED OFFICERS
30.18 On the proposal for re-employment of retired officers, the Director, CBI stated thus:–

28
Re-employment will not affect promotion. Sir, we have quotas. So, the re-employment is
only against the vacancies where we are not able to promote officers to that level. It is not
that we are depriving or keeping somebody out of promotion. That will not happen. These are
only the re-employments where there is no r ecruitment and there is nobody to take these posts.
So, only those people are being re-employed. It does not affect the promotion prospects or
recruitment prospects of anybody in the organization.
30.19 One of the Members expressed his opinion in this regard as follows:–
If only those who have retired or who are going to retire, are again inducted or engaged,
the young blood will not come. There will always be old blood. This can be done for a short
period of time. But that should not be there for all times to come.
30.20 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that urgent steps should be taken to
address the issue of vacant posts. The Committee feels that engaging persons on contract basis
or on re-employment are only ad-hoc measures and that they should not be resorted to as a
practice. The Committee is of the view that the accountability of persons appointed on ad-hoc
basis will be lesser than the regular employees and more so, in an agency such as CBI, where
confidentiality is a major factor. Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
taken to address the existing problems, in a holistic manner and that piece-meal measures
should not be resorted to. The fact that eligible officers are not available in the organization
is indicative of the fact that the cadre management in the CBI, had at stages, suffered
mismanagement. This needs to be paid adequate attention so that such situations do not
happen again.
(iv) STATUTORY BACK-UP FOR CBI
30.21 Regarding requisite statutory support for CBI, the Ministry has stated in its reply that:–
1. To the query whether by virtue of Entry 8 in the Union List, it is open to the Central
Government to constitute a CBI for purpose of investigating into any offences related
to a matter in the Union List with a view to launch prosecution, A.G . has opined that
it is too broadly stated. It would be necessary to identify the matters in the Union List,
which the proposed legislation would relate to. In any case, it is not open to the Central
Government to constitute, a CBI and confer on it powers which will impinge all the
powers of investigation of offences which are conferred on the State police.
2. He has further stated that it is not open to provide that the jurisdiction of the bureau
shall extend to whole of India and that prior consent of the States will not be necessary.
In his opinion, this violates the basic federal structure of the Constitution.
3. A.G . has also stated that the amendment envisaged in the Bill will have the effect of
altering the basic structure of the Constitution and its federal character.
4. With regard to the query whether there is any other way to create an independent
corruption investigation agency in India without compromising the federal set up/basic
features of the Constitution, A.G . has stated that it cannot be answered in a vacuum as
it depends on the nature of the proposed legislation.
30.22 The Committee takes note of the opinion of the learned A.G. But, it is noteworthy that
a federal legislation, viz., The National Investigation Agency Act, 2008 is in place, which
provides for an investigation agency at the national level to investigate and prosecute certain
class of offences. The Committee is of the considered view that a legislation may be proposed
on similar lines, to give an effective statutory backing to CBI, which is a dire need of the
hour, while taking care that the basic features of the Constitution are not compromised.

The requirement projected by CBI for various schemes/activities could not be considered

hampered due to budgetary constraints.
(vi) PENDENCY OF CASES
30.27 On the issue of pendency of cases in CBI, the Director, CBI deposed thus:–
...the DoPT is in the process of forming a Committee. And, it is better if this is done

(vii) MEDICAL FACILITIES TO CBI  PERSONNEL
30.29 The Ministry, in its Action taken reply furnished on the 24
th Report of this Committee, has
stated that the medical and clinical facilities available to the CBI officers and their families are at

present the same as provided to other Central Government employees by the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare.
30.30 However, the Committee takes note of the deposition of Director, CBI that better medical facilities
should be extended to CBI personnel because of work related stress, characteristic of their job.
30.31 The Committee agrees to the fact that the CBI personnel are engaged in stressful work
unrelentingly and that the medical facilities extended to them are inadequate. Since the CGHS
facilities are available during working hours only and on working days and the CBI personnel
may not be able to avail these facilities due to the hectic schedule of their work or outstation

tight and tough work schedule.

30.32 The Director, CBI while deposing before the Committee, stressed upon the need to have

that measures may also be taken to provide every CBI Branch with a Forensic Evidence

to ensure that the state-of-the art technology is available for the best collection of evidence
at all relevant stages, unlike the present arrangement, where the CBI is reliant on the
Forensic Science Laboratories which are beyond its control.

DEPARTMENTAL EXAMINATION
32.1 It has been s tated in the Annual Report of the Ministry that eight (out of nine) regional offices

35

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
Reduced expenditure at RE stage
1. The Committee is constrained to note the low level of expenditure/non-expenditure of
various Plan funds due to non-finalization of schemes/delay in implementation of various
schemes. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the reasons furnished by the
Ministry for reducing the expenditure at the RE stage, under the above mentioned vital Plan
Schemes for the last three years, have remained almost the same. The Committee wonders
why this trend was not noticed and arrested by taking appropriate remedial steps. The
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that such causes, when once identified, should have been
carefully evaluated and remedial steps should have been taken in anticipation so that they did
not recur. The Committee is of the considered view that since the Ministry is a crucial agency
dealing with the human resources of the Government and other important Central Policies/
Schemes, optimum utilization of available funds should be ensured, or otherwise, reductions at
the RE stage in this manner can be seen as a reflection on the efficiency of the Ministry.
[Para 6.3]
2. The Committee recommends that such laches should be avoided to the extent possible,
and that steps should be taken in advance to ensure that such delays do not impede
development and modernization. The Committee is of the view that agencies and individuals
should be made accountable for such delays. [Para 6.5]
3. The Committee is of the considered opinion that when funds were made available to the
organization so liberally for the purpose of engaging consultants, the latter should have shown
matching degree of enthusiasm and initiative to see that the activities for which funds were
provided were accomplished. The Committee feels that periodic evaluation by the Ministry of
the progress of such schemes can go a long way in avoiding such happenings. [Para 6.7]
4. The Committee feels that CBI, being a premier agency, should have well thought out
proposals and realistic plan of action regarding utilization of funds, more particularly the Plan
funds, which are imperative for growth and development, so that such non-utilisation/under-
utilisation do not occur in future. [Para 6.11]
5. The Committee notes the allocations made by the Ministry to UPSC. [Para 7.1.2]

16. The Committee recommends that the suggestions made in the Study should be given
proper thought and consideration, particularly those relating to sensitization of PIOs and
speedier disposal. The Ministry’s scheme for training of PIOs, may be a good step. It is also

conclusion. [Para 17.3]
17. The Committee feels that measures such as effective training of PIOs, publicity
campaigns, more proactive disclosure, better record management and more infrastructure for
public authorities are extremely important to ensure that the maximum benefit of the RTI Act
accrue to the public. [Para 17.4]
18. The Committee further takes note of the suggestion made in the Study that e-Hearing
of cases may be adopted for speedy disposal. The Committee takes cognizance of the
recommendation made in the Study that third party audits should be commissioned by the
Information Commissions to empanelled civil society organizations. [Para 17.5]
19. With regard to achieving the objective of the RTI Act, the Committee is of the
considered view that much of it depends upon the proper implementation of the provisions of
Section 4 of the Act relating to proactive disclosur es. The RTI Act casts an obligation on every
Public Authority to provide as much information in the public domain on an ongoing basis so
that public have minimum resort to the use of this Act for obtaining information. The
Committee feels that quite a lot needs to be done in so far as implementation of the provisions
of Section 4(2) of the RTI Act is concerned. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the
Ministry should come out with a specific and time bound programme whereunder, the various
Public Authorities should examine threadbare what all information available with them or
generated in the course of their functioning should be placed in public domain. Further, in
order to ensure that the said programme progresses as per schedule, the Ministry should also
provide for monitoring of the action taken by various public authorities in compliance of the
said provisions of the RTI Act. The Committee feels that once this initial exercise is undertaken,
it would not be burdensome for the Public Authorities to update/add to the said information
on an ongoing basis. [Para 17.6]
OVERSTAY WHILE ON DEPUTATION
20. The Committee feels that deputation, as a policy, has been envisaged to facilitate
mobility of personnel between Departments so that the concerned person as well as the
Department(s) benefit from the process. When the person on deputation reverts to his parent
Department, he can put to use the innovative practices that he imbibed from the other
Department and also, the latter can derive benefits from the processes followed in the person’s
parent Department. Therefore, once the period of deputation is over, it is beyond reason that
the person overstays. The Committee is of the considered view that the existing tendency of

41
treating deputation as a tool by persons considering certain places uncomfortable, to ensure
posting in a better place, or to get a hometown posting, should be discouraged. The Committee
hopes that the above-mentioned step taken by the Ministry would help in curbing such
tendencies. [Para 18.1]
21. The Committee in this context further observes that there are umpteen instances of
Government officials remaining on deputation for years together, moving from one department
of Government to another and even to other statutory/autonomous organizations and their
stay in their parent organization remains very limited. The Committee is of the considered
view that the instrument of deputation does serve public interest only if the deputations take
place in departments/organizations where the qualification and work experience of the
deputationist officer are relevant and secondly, the deputation continues for a reasonable
period within which the borrowing department/organization is able to benefit from the
experience/exposure of the deputationist officer. When deputations take place and continue
in violation of these conditions, the Committee feels that, in such cases, the instrument of
deputation is being misused for personal gain by the deputationist officer. Such tendencies
need to be curbed with a strong hand. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry
has issued strict guidelines against unauthorized overstay while on deputation. The Committee
in this context feels that the instructions issued by the Ministry may be made applicable on
the lending Government departments from where Government officials go on deputation to
different statutory/autonomous bodies of Government of India. Such an action, the Committee
feels, would be able to regulate and conform the deputation of all Government officials to
the desired objective. [Para 18.2]

the accomplishment of this mission, it becomes imperative on the part of the DoPT to ensure

recruitment as well as promotions in the different Services under the Government of India
which are under the control and supervision of the DoPT. [Para 25.0]

the I.A.S., the Central Secretariat Services and the Group A Services. The Committee

being paid from the Government exchequer. Such an action, the Committee feels, would be in

for the Government of India and advising the Ministries/Departments in the implementation
of the same. [Para 25.1]
30. The Committee, however, does not see this reduction in the workforce in the Government
sector as a healthy trend. In Committee’s view, such a trend can have major negative
implications, compared to the meager benefits of savings on account of putting in place a
leaner administration. The Committee further feels that the shortage of workforce is being
felt evenly in the various Government establishments leading to engagement of workforce on
contract basis and also outsourcing some of its activities. This also includes engaging of retired
Government officials in all types of Government establishments. The Committee does not see
this to be a healthy trend because the level of accountability of these contract appointees is
definitely lesser than regular appointees in Government. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that the DoPT may ascertain the magnitude of re-employment/contractual
employment in all types of Government establishments falling under their mandate and find

common man while dealing with Government Departments. [Para 27.6]
DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
37. The Committee appreciates this initiative of the Department. [Para 28.2]
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
(i) ONLINE RECEIVING OF APPLICATION
38. The Committee appreciates the step taken by UPSC which is beneficial to candidates.
The Committee hopes that this would cut short the overall time taken in the conduct of the
examination. [Para 29.3]
(iii) DELAY IN SENDING OFFERS OF APPOINTMENT
39. The Committee is happy to note that UPSC has taken cognizance of this week area
in Government’s functioning. The Committee recommends that the concerned Ministries
should take serious note of such delays and that they should devise appropriate measures
to ensure that candidates recommended by UPSC, are issued offers of appointment, without
delay. [Para 29.6]

44
(iv) DELAY IN NOTIFICATION OF RECRUITMENT RULES
40. The Committee is of the view that such delay in notification hinders the recruitment
process and therefore, desires that the Ministries/Departments should take due care and
caution to make sure that such delays do not occur. Absence of Recruitment Rules eventually
pave way for ad hoc actions and mal-exercise of discretion which are totally undesirable. The
Committee recommends proactive action on the part of the Ministry in this very important
area. [Para 29.8]
(v) CONDUCT OF ON-LINE RECRUITMENT TEST
41. The Committee desires that steps should be taken by UPSC to ensure that the time
taken for disposing recruitment cases is reduced, by proper management of resources and
taking advantage of the latest technological advancements. [Para 29.12]
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
(i) V ACANCIES IN CBI
42. The Committee would like to place on record its deep anguish over the vacancies
existing in CBI at various levels. The Committee is perturbed to note that inspite of its
repeated recommendations on this issue, in its various Reports on Demands for Grants of the
Ministry of Personnel and its 24
th Report on “Working of CBI”, the situation, instead of
improving, has progressively worsened. [Para 30.6]
43. The Committee fails to understand how, the country’s premier investigating agency,
whose mandate has witnessed an unprecedented increase in the recent years, can be expected
to function efficiently and keep up with the high expectations placed on it by the public,
judiciary and legislature, with such a large shortfall of manpower on several important posts.
The situation is beyond justification because in the proposed Lokpal regime, the role of CBI
in investigating corruption cases is bound to expand tremendously. Therefore, CBI can ill
afford to have such large number of vacancies. The Committee strongly feels it to be a matter
of serious concern that the officers and staff of CBI, who are already under immense stress
and strain, will surely not be able to keep pace with the workload, if the vacancies continue
to exist. [Para 30.7]
44. The Committee strongly recommends that strategic steps should be taken on a war
footing, with strict deadlines fixed and the Ministry, in co-ordination with CBI, should devise
measures to fill up these vacancies. Also, measures should be adopted in a planned manner,
to create a conducive working environment so that new talent is attracted to join the
organization. The Committee desires that it should be apprised of the steps taken in this
regard, in the Action taken reply. [Para 30.8]
(ii) DEPENDENCE ON THE OFFICERS ON DEPUTATION
45.  The Committee does not find merit in the argument put forward that if officers from
States’ Police are not taken on deputation in CBI, this will give rise to the suspicion of
branding CBI as agency of Central Government and also may lead to withholding of consent
under DSPE Act by the State Governments. The Committee does not find any logic in such
an argument. The act of giving consent by the State for investigation into a case depends on
the nature of the crime, gravity of the offence, etc. The Committee fails to understand how
the presence of deputationists in CBI, is in any way, likely to improve the decision-making
process in this regard. [Para 30.11]

45
46. The Committee strongly feels that the good reputation that CBI currently enjoys due
to its pretty reasonable conviction rate, can also be attributed to the commendable way in
which departmental officers, whose skills have been honed to deal with specialized and
complicated crimes, owing to their continuous exposure to such cases, have ensured successful
investigation and prosecution. [Para 30.12]
47. The Committee strongly feels that this submission is beyond justification. It is of the
considered view that investigation skills that are expected from an officer of CBI are inherently
different from those expected from a police officer posted in the States. The very fact that,
when the State police fails to solve a case, it is referred to CBI, suggests that the skills
expected of a CBI officer are different and specialized. Therefore, the Committee strongly
recommends that the departmental officers in CBI should form and continue to form the
backbone of the organisation and that any attempt to dilute their strength should be strongly
discouraged and resisted. [Para 30.14]
48. The Committee is of the view that by giving sufficient training and exposure to the
departmental officers in various fields, they will, over a period of time, evolve into experts in
such fields. So, greater emphasis should be given to steps such as skill enhancement of the
CBI departmental personnel, rather than encouraging deputation. Induction of deputationists
in CBI should be strictly on a selective and merit basis aimed to instill talent and skill in the
organization and it should not be a routine exercise of filling up deputation quota from the
States. [Para 30.15]
49. The Committee is of the considered view that in order to attract fresh talent, a
conducive working environment and adequate promotional prospects are vital factors. The
Committee feels that in order to ensure a satisfactory working environment, the departmental
officers of CBI should be actively involved in the medium and long term decision policy
making processes in CBI so that they are adequately groomed to hold higher responsibilities.
The Committee would also like to emphasize the dire need of protecting the promotional
interests of the departmental officers in CBI and recommends that steps should be taken to
avoid stagnation at various levels where posts are manned by departmental officers.
[Para 30.17]
(iii) RE-EMPLOYMENT OF RETIRED OFFICERS
50. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that urgent steps should be taken to
address the issue of vacant posts. The Committee feels that engaging persons on contract basis
or on re-employment are only ad-hoc measures and that they should not be resorted to as a
practice. The Committee is of the view that the accountability of persons appointed on ad-hoc
basis will be lesser than the regular employees and more so, in an agency such as CBI, where
confidentiality is a major factor. Therefore, the Committee recommends that steps should be
taken to address the existing problems, in a holistic manner and that piece-meal measures
should not be resorted to. The fact that eligible officers are not available in the organization
is indicative of the fact that the cadre management in the CBI, had at stages, suffered
mismanagement. This needs to be paid adequate attention so that such situations do not
happen again. [Para 30.20]
(iv) STATUTORY BACK-UP FOR CBI
51. The Committee takes note of the opinion of the learned A.G. But, it is noteworthy
that a federal legislation, viz., The National Investigation Agency Act, 2008 is in place, which
provides for an investigation agency at the national level to investigate and prosecute certain

46
class of offences. The Committee is of the considered view that a legislation may be proposed
on similar lines, to give an effective statutory backing to CBI, which is a dire need of the
hour, while taking care that the basic features of the Constitution are not compromised.
[Para 30.22]
(v) MODERNISATION OF CBI
52. The Committee strongly feels that shortage of funds should, as far as possible, not be
a reason for delay in modernization and upgradation of the premier investigating agency,
whose mandate is increasing with the passage of time. The Committee is of the view that the
Ministry should ensure that the efficient functioning of CBI should not be allowed to be
hampered due to budgetary constraints. [Para 30.26]
(vi) PENDENCY OF CASES
53. The Committee takes note of the initiative and desires that the proposed Committee
should be formed without delay, to review the pending cases, so that the real pendency gets
identified and efforts are directed pointedly on them for their resolution. [Para 30.28]
(vii) MEDICAL FACILITIES TO CBI PERSONNEL
54. The Committee agrees to the fact that the CBI personnel are engaged in stressful work
unrelentingly and that the medical facilities extended to them are inadequate. Since the CGHS
facilities are available during working hours only and on working days and the CBI personnel
may not be able to avail these facilities due to the hectic schedule of their work or outstation
travels, the present system seems to be grossly inadequate. Therefore, the Committee strongly
recommends that the Ministry should put in place a health care mechanism for CBI officers
and staff, on the lines of those available for paramilitary personnel on a 24x7 basis, so that
they get proper medical and clinical access. The Committee feels that the proposition that the
CBI personnel are entitled to only such benefits as other Central Government employees, does
not hold good because of the difference in the nature of work they engage in and also their
tight and tough work schedule. [Para 30.31]
(vii) FORENSIC EVIDENCE COLLECTION UNITS
55. The Committee feels that collection and analysis of forensic evidence is of vital
importance for investigation and successful prosecution. Therefore, the Committee recommends
that measures may also be taken to provide every CBI Branch with a Forensic Evidence
Collection Unit, complete with necessary skilled manpower, dedicated equipment and resources
to ensure that the state-of-the art technology is available for the best collection of evidence
at all relevant stages, unlike the present arrangement, where the CBI is reliant on the
Forensic Science Laboratories which are beyond its control. [Para 30.33]
(viii) DEMAND FOR JOINT DIRECTOR (NORTH EAST)
56. The Committee appreciates this step and hopes that the genuine demands made by CBI
will continue to get positive and due consideration by the Ministry. [Para 30.35]
(ix) ANTI-HUMAN TRAFFICKING CELL
57. The Committee takes note of this demand. The Committee is of the considered opinion
that since human trafficking crimes quite often cross State boundaries and have inter-State

47
ramifications, it is imperative that a separate Cell is formed in CBI to exclusively deal with
such crimes. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Government should consider this
proposal on an urgent basis. [Para 30.37]
(x) TRAINING ON STRESS MANAGEMENT
58. The Committee wishes to emphasize upon the need for imparting training on Stress
Management techniques to the CBI personnel. [Para 30.39]
59. The Committee is heartened to note that training for officers of South East Asian
Countries also is held in the CBI Academy at Ghaziabad. The Committee hopes that the
proposed modernisation of the Academy will enable it to be transformed to a word class
institution. [Para 30.40]
(xi) ANTI-CORRUPTION AWARENESS PROGRAMME
60. The Committee appreciates this initiative. [Para 30.42]
(xii) CBI SPECIAL COURTS
61. The Committee notes that 54 CBI Special Courts have become functional. The Committee
would like to impress upon the Ministry to take steps to ensure that all the 71 Special Courts
become functional and also to take steps to fill the existing vacancies of judges in the Special
Courts. [Para 30.44]
CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
62. The Committee hopes that such a measure will help in reducing pendency of cases in
the CAT. [Para 31.2]
STAFF SELECTION COMMISSION
DEPARTMENTAL EXAMINATION
63. The Committee appreciates this milestone achieved by SSC. [Para 32.2]
64. The Committee notes the initiatives taken by SSC and is pleased to see other organizations
seeking SSC’s assistance for holding their recruitment exams and also entrusting conduct of
examinations to them. [Para 32.6]
65. The Committee appreciates the Commission’s decision to post marks of qualifying and
non-qualifying candidates on its website, resulting in greater transparency and interaction
between the candidates and the Commission. The Committee feels that such initiatives enhance
the confidence of the candidates in the integrity of the recruiting agency. [Para 32.7]
66. The Committee takes note of the above mentioned steps taken by SSC to evolve itself
into a candidate friendly recruiting agency. [Para 32.11]
67. The Committee takes note of the replies and desires that upgradation activities should
be taken up in a planned manner. [Para 32.15]
LAL BAHADUR SHASTRI NATIONAL ACADEMY OF ADMINISTRATION
68. …The Committee hopes that such activities will help in creating a sense of empathy
in the minds of officer trainees. [Para 33.2]

48
69. The Committee appreciates the steps taken for improvement of infrastructure and
upgradation of LBSNAA to a Centre of Excellence. The Committee stresses upon the need
for Stress Management training programmes to be included in the syllabus of LBSNAA.
[Para 33.3]
KENDRIYA BHANDAR
70. The Committee appreciates such initiatives. [Para 34.2]
71. The Committee is heartened to note that the sales of Rs. 461.38 crores achieved by
Kendriya Bhandar during 2010-11 is the highest ever sales achieved by it so far. The Committee
reiterates its recommendations contained in its 30
th and 42 nd Reports on this institution.
[Para 34.3]
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
72. The Committee took serious note of the acute shortage of manpower in the CVC
particularly in view of the large number of organizations and employee strength of these
organisations that come under its purview, as mentioned in its Annual Report. [Para 35.1]
73. The Committee considers this a serious situation and apprehends that the efficiency of
the Commission is going to suffer. The Committee also takes note of CVC’s enhanced demand
of Rs. 1.87 crore. The Committee hopes that CVC will prioritize the filling up of vacant
positions in a phased manner. [Para 35.1.B]
74. The Committee recommends that the concerns put forward by CVC should be given
foremost attention by the Ministry, keeping in view the vital role expected to be played by
CVC in the proposed Lokpal regime. The Committee desires that the Ministry should give
necessary assistance to CVC in order to ensure that it emerges as the principal vigilance
machinery in the country, equipped to provide efficient administrative vigilance in all the
organizations which come under its fold. [Para 35.4]
75. The Committee takes note of the positive steps taken by CVC to ensure speedy
sanction for prosecution on CBI reports. [Para 35.5]
76. The Committee reckons the above-mentioned measures taken by CVC to fulfill its
mandate in the right sprit and also hopes that these steps would enable to ensure an
administration with zero tolerance to corruption. [Para 35.9]
CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION
77. The Committee takes note of the deposition made by Secretary, CIC and impresses
upon the Ministry to take up the issue with the concerned agencies and expedite the process.
[Para 36.2]
78. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that requisite manpower and
infrastructure should be provided for CIC so that it can fulfill its statutory mandate to the
best extent possible. [Para 36.6]
SANSKRITI SCHOOL
79. The Committee takes note of the information submitted by the Ministry. [Para 37.4]

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three Departments, namely the Department
of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice and through the said Departments,
the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards realisation of the objectives set
out in the Constitution.
Department of Legal Affairs
1.1 The Department of Legal Affairs is essentially a service Department that renders advice to
various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal matters and carries out the
litigation work in various Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besides this, it is also concerned with
appointment of Law Officers, namely the Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India and the
Additional Solicitor Generals of India, entering into treaties with foreign countries in matters of Civil
law inclusive of Hague Convention Matters, executing contracts and assurances of property on behalf
of the President of India. It is also the nodal authority in respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign
Exchange, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal.
1.2 The Department of Legal Affairs has a two tier set up, namely, the Main Secretariat, New
Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The nature of duties
discharged by the Main Secretariat as well as Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into two
areas – Advice work and Litigation work. Advice caters to Central Government Department/Offices at
Centre and in States/UTs. Litigation work relates to CAT, High Courts and Supreme Court.
1.3 The following are the organisations/institutions, which come under the overall supervision of
Department of Legal Affairs and get Grant in aid for their research works:–
(a) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) :– The National Legal Services Authority
has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to monitor and
evaluate implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down policies and principles
for making legal services available under the Act. The NALSA issues guidelines for the
State Legal Services Authorities to implement the legal aid programmes which are in turn
discharged through the following services:–
(i) Free Legal Services :– It includes court fees, process fee and all charges payable
or incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing Advocate in legal
proceedings, obtaining and supply of rectified copies of orders and other documents
in legal proceedings, preparation of appeal, paper book including printing and translation
of documents in legal proceedings.
(ii) Lok Adalats:– Lok Adalat is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in the court
of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably. The Lok Adalat
has been given statutory status under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
Under this Act, an award made by a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil
court and is final and binding on all parties and no appeal lies against thereto before
any court.

2
(b) Law Commission of India :– The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body,
constituted by the Government once in three years. The Commission was first constituted
in 1955. It consists of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one Member-Secretary and
three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature of work. Law Commission
Reports are considered to be primary source of law reforms for Parliament, as well as
the judiciary. Law Commission presents its Report to the Government, the Government
then lays these Reports on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
(c) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT):– Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961
provides that the Central Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal consisting of
as many Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit, to exercise the
powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate Tribunal by said Act.
(d) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange :– The Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange
was established on 1
st June, 2000 vide Government of India Notification No. S.O. 531
(E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act,
1999 (FEMA),
(e) Indian Law Institute (ILI) :– The Indian Law Institute registered under the Societies
Registration Act, 1860 is engaged in research in the field of law. The Department of Legal
Affairs has been sanctioning annual recurring Grant in aid to the Institute for its activities
of legal research.
(f) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR) :– The International
Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the Societies Registration
Act, 1860 on 31
st May, 1995. It is an autonomous organisation working under the aegis
of the Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs). It has been established
to promote, organise and propagate alternative dispute resolution methods to facilitate
early resolution of disputes and to reduce the burden of arrears on Courts.
(g) Bar Council of India (BCI) :– The Bar Council of India is a statutory body constituted
under the Advocates Act 1961. The Council has been receiving annual Grant in aid from
Department of Legal Affairs.
(h) Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) :– The Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies is a private body engaged in research in the field
of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies and came into existence in 1965. The
Department of Legal Affairs has been sanctioning recurring annual Grant in aid to the
Institute for the purpose.
Legislative Department
1.4 The Legislative Department is entrusted with legislative matters and is responsible for drafting of
all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and vetting of subordinate legislations sponsored by
various Union Ministries/ Departments. It is also administratively concerned with certain matters such as
the Code of Civil Procedure, Limitation and Arbitration, Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer
of Property as regards legislation. There are over hundred Central Acts falling under these subjects.
1.5 The Department has two wings under it mainly:-
(i) Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research : With a view to increase the availability
of trained legislative draftsmen in the country, the Institute of Legislative Drafting and
Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and
Justice in January, 1989. The Institute has been imparting theoretical as well as practical
training in legislative drafting.

3
(ii) Of ficial Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The Official Languages Wing
is a successor Organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission under the
Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the functions such as, (a) to prepare
and publish a standard legal terminology for use, as far as possible, in all Official
Languages; (b) to prepare authoritative texts in Hindi of all Central Acts and Ordinances
and Regulations promulgated by the President; (c) to prepare authoritative texts in Hindi
of all rules, regulations and orders made by the Central Government under any Central
Act or any Ordinance or Regulation promulgated by the President; (d) to prepare
authoritative texts of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the
President in the respective Official Languages of the States and to arrange for the
translation of all Acts passed and Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the
texts of such Acts or Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi; and (e) to perform
such other duties as may be assigned to it by the Government of India from time to time.
1.6 Election Commission of India : Legislative Department is also administratively concerned with
the Election Commission of India and Election laws connected with election to Parliament and State
Legislatures and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President. There is a separate Demand
NO.61 for the Election Commission of India.
Department of Justice
1.7 The duties of the Department of Justice include the administration of justice and the processing
of appointment of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
1.8 The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come directly under the overall
supervision of Department of Justice:
(a) Supreme Court of India :– There is a separate demand No.64 (Appropriation) pertaining
to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of
India is ‘Charged’ expenditure.
(b) National Judicial Academy :– The National Judicial Academy was registered as a Society
under the Societies Registration Act and came into existence with effect from 17
th August,
1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing Council, which is chaired
by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the Academy is in Supreme Court
Building at New Delhi and another office was established in August, 2000 at Bhopal. The
main objectives of the Academy are to impart training to the Judicial Officers of the
States/Union territories and to study the court management and administration of justice
in States and Union territories.
(c) E-courts. Mission Mode Project Phase-II :– This is a new Scheme proposed in the
Twelfth Plan which is built upon the experience of the E-courts Project Phase I with new
components such as Computerisation of 1000 new Courts, Use of Solar energy under e-
Courts Project, Computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office, Videoconferencing
facility for Jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of Courts, Digitization of old case
records, Computerisation of Judicial libraries, up gradation of application software, SMS
Based Services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of Rs. 1280 crore which would
be spread over a period of five years.
(d) Family Courts :– The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a view to providing for
establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation in and secure speedy settlement
of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related matters. These Courts are civil
in nature, establishment of which has direct bearing on the reduction of pendency of civil
suits in various High Courts. In accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act,

4
the State/UT Governments can establish Family Courts in the areas comprising districts,
towns, city in the States having population of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs are
competent to establish such court in those areas with the State/UT having a population
less than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.
(e) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :– The
Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for the
establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of providing
speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps. In so far as
the Central Government is concerned, it is committed to provide assistance to the State
Governments for meeting the non-recurring cost of establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas.
The Central Government would also meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred
on these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of Rs. 3.20 lakhs per annum.

the shortfall, the Ministry informed the Committee that the present allocations to the Ministry under

2.5 The Committee notes that the budget allocated to the Ministry in the Plan side is as
per the demands projected while there exist a meager shortfall in the Non-Plan allocation.
While the Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry in following the guidelines of the
Ministry of Finance to take austerity measures in expenditure, it is also of the considered view
that the efficient and smooth functioning of the Government machinery should not be
compromised. The Committee, during it’s interaction with the various autonomous bodies and
institutions under the Ministry’s administrative control, was informed of the shortage of funds
and thereby adversely affecting their performance. In that backdrop, the Committee hopes
that the Ministry will be judicious in the utilisation of the budgetary allocation.

started in 2011-12, no amount was kept for the scheme in the year 2011-12. Hence, a major increase
